10 Body-parts and emotional behaviors 
Chapter 7 to 9 described how a number of Dalabon compound predicates denoting 
emotions and involving body-parts may be interpreted in terms of tropes ( either 
metonymies or metaphors). With these sets of compounds, the tropes in question are the 
best candidates for historical motivation of these compounds: they explain the structure of 
the sets, and the existence of some compounds could hardly be explained by any 
alternative factor. However, not all Dalabon emotional compounds are motivated by 
conceptual tropes. As pointed out by numerous studies on lexical semantics and semantic 
change (among many others, Cruse (1986), Traugott & Dasher (2002)), conceptual 
metaphors and metonymies are by no means the only motivation to produce new words 
and assign meaning to them. This chapter highlights the role of strictly formal, or 
structural (i.e. not conceptual) paths of word formation and semantic change, namely 
principles related to compositionality and formal analogy. 
Here 'compositionality
1 
refers to the regular processes of sense computation in a given 
language, i.e. the rules that apply to co_mpute the sense of new compounds in a predictable 
way. In Dalabon, the sense of a lexeme is for instance compositional when a compound 
follows the standard rules of noun incorporation; or more broadly, if the sense of a 
compound can be predicted based on combinations recurrent elsewhere in the language. 
In this chapter, I will show that (semi-)compositionality plays a role in several sets of 
emotional behavior compounds. I call any [noun+predicate] associations a 'compound
1
: 
the word 'compound
1 
refers to formal pairings, irrespective of the semantic or syntactic 
relationships between the items in question. 
I call 'formal analogy
1 
the processes by which speakers draw inspiration from existing 
forms in the language, to produce new forms or realign existing forms ( as commonly 
,..., 360,..., 
[PDF PAGE 386]
Chapter 10 · • Body-parts and emotional behaviors 
occurs across paradigms (see for instance Campbell (2004:Chapter 10)). 1 In Dalabon, this 
applies for instance when speakers reproduce the structure of some [ noun+predicate] 
compounds to create another [ noun+predicate] compound. As an example, mud-kele-mun 
'body hair'+'FEAR'+INCH me_ans 'scared' (goosebumps somatic metonymy) and djong-bruk 
'FEAR'+'dry' means 'brave'. Drawing from these two compounds, mud-bruk 'body 
hair'+'dry' means 'brave' as well. The form of the last compound is inspired by formal 
analogy with djong-bruk 'be brave': the compounds are structurally equivalent, and they 
present the same form. Mud-bruk 'body hair'+'dry' is all the more natural in that [body­
part+emotion/behavior predicates] are frequent throughout the sets described below. 
Formal analogy is accompanied by semantic analogy: the semantic connotations gained by 
MUD 'body hair' in mud-kele-mun 'be scared' are transferred to another compound. In this 
chapter, I show how various sets of predicates related to emotional behaviors display 
family resemblances: the sets are extended and new sets are created by virtue of formal 
analogy with other sets. 
In the following sections I describe six semi-productive sets of emotional compounds of 
the type [body-part+predicate] or [attribute of the person+predicate] having to do with 
emotional behaviors, in which recurrent semantic contrasts are observed. In addition, 
although each set differs from the others, they display family-resemblance analogies . Some 
of the compounds in these sets are metonymic or metaphoric, ~ut many compounds are 
also essentially (semi-)compositional. While I will show how these processes or lexical 
production and semantic extension operate within each set, I am not concerned so much 
with the variety and details of the processes in question. Instead, my point is that 
compositionality and formal analogy, rather than conceptual metaphors and metonymies, 
constitute the main motivation for compound formation and semantic shift in these sets. 
That is, aside from conceptual motivations, formal principles are also the source of various 
semantic extensions and shifts, in particular conferring emotional senses to visible body­
part nouns and to a few predicates. In addition, I suggest that the compounds produced on 
the basis of these formal principles may in turn inspire conceptual metaphors to speakers, 
so that formal principals may be the source of conceptual representations, rather than 
only the reverse. 
1 Such processes are usually called simply 'analogy', but in the context of this study , this would 
entail a confusion with conceptual analogy as the underlying principle of metaphors, hence the 
specification as 'formal analogy'.

[PDF PAGE 387]
The language of emotions in Dalabon 
In Section 1, I discuss a number of emotional-behavior compound predicates, and how 
they are organized in semi-productive sets of compounds where a significant proportion 
of the compounds can be interpreted as noun incorporation constructions. The sets share 
two main structural properties. Firstly, in these semi-productive sets, visible body-parts 
are used to specify which part of the body of the experiencer of the emotion is involved in 
the behavior related to the emotion. Secondly, invisible body-parts ( organs, bones) and 
abstract attributes of the person tend to specify predicates as emotional, as opposed to 
behavioral. Within these sets, many compounds attract semi-compositional 
interpretations, following the rules of noun incorporation (see Chapter 3, 2.3). Some 
compounds move away from it, which in turn results in the semantic reanalysis of some of 
the components. Section 1.4 questions how such sets may be interpreted metaphorically, 
although there are reasons to think that they are not motivated historically by metaphors, 
but by compositionality and analogy. As a result, in this case, linguistic metaphors may 
suggest conceptual metaphors, rather than the reverse. 
Another semantic consequence of these emotional behavior sets is that, because there are 
several sets of this type with some family resemblances, they reiterate regular contrasts, 
and this contributes to establishing new meanings for the reiterated nouns. These 
extensions are discussed in Section 2. This is how an invisible body-part like KANGU 
'belly', the effect of which, in the sets, is to specify the predicate as emotional, becomes 
closely associated with emotions-consistent with its role in the metaphors described in 
Chapter 8. 
1. Emotional behavior sets 
It was noted in Chapter 8 that while metaphors for emotions involving body-parts concern 
a large number of predicates, they do not concern a very large number of body-parts: 
mainly the belly, and the heart (see Chapter 8). However, Dalabon features many more 
body-part compounds related to emotions, and more specifically to emotional behaviors. 
Emotional behaviors are behaviors that are regularly associated with an emotion. 
Emotional behavior predicates, as defined in Chapter 1 (1.2.2.3), are predicates which 
describe a behavior, but also imply, as part of their sense, the emotional trigger of this 
emotion. For example, yer{mu) 'avoid interactions for fear of others' describes avoidance 
,...., 362,...., 
[PDF PAGE 388]
Chapter 10 • Body-parts and emotional behaviors 
behaviors, but implies that avoidance results from certain emotions such as fear or 
respect, as opposed to avoiding someone because one finds them boring, for instance). 
There are several semi-productive sets of the form [body-part+emotional behavior 
predicate], yielding predicates like dalu-yer(mu) 'mouth'+'avoid interaction for fear of 
others', 'be too shy to talk'. A large number of these compounds are, like dalu-yer(mu), 
largely compositional in form and meaning, i.e. they obey the rules of syntactic 
incorporation. The incorporated body-part specifies which part of the absolutive 
argument (S for intransitive emotional predicates) is involved in the behavior in question: 
ngah-dalu-yer(mu), literally 'I'm ashamed from the mouth'.

In most cases, the sense of such compounds remains essentially compositional, repeating 
comparable semantic specifications: the resulting compound predicate is a behavioral 
hyponym of the simple emotional behavior predicate, specifying the behavior in question 
via the body-part involved in this behavior. 2 Hence dalu-yer(mu) 'be too shy to talk' is a 
hyponym of yer(mu) 'avoid interaction for fear of others', specifying behavior related to 
the mouth. The relation between the incorporated body-part and the specified behavior is 
not entirely _ predictable. With da/u-yer(mu), the compound picks a function of da/u-no 
'mouth' (i.e. speech). With kokmele-yer(mu) '?cheek, temple'+'avoid interaction for fear of 
others', 'turn head to avoid someone's look', it is the body-part involved in the posture that 
contributes the semantic specification. 
Some of these compounds are occasional and not lexicalized. Others may be regarded as 
partly lexicalized to the extent that they are frequent, in spite of the fact that their 
lexicalized sense is compositional. Other compounds are fully lexicalized, since they 
receive a non-compositional lexical interpretation, which may in turn trigger metaphorical

general. 
1.1 Yirru 'conflict', 'anger' 
Table 1 lists compounds of the form [noun+YIRRU predicate], where the predicate can be

different contribution here than in dalu-yer(mu) 'too shy to talk'. The resulting compounds 
are behavioral hyponyms of the predicate, meaning 'express anger by means of body-part 
· X'. Thus, the relation between the alternating nouns and the recurring predicates are 
regular, or at least semi-regular: the set is structured by principles of compositionality.

1.1.1 Invisible body-parts and attributes of the person 
Not all compounds in Table 1 are hyponyms of YIRRU 'conflict, anger' predicates. In fact, 
none of the compounds formed with nouns which are not visible body-parts is a hyponym 
of YIRRU predicates. Some of these compounds are formed with invisible parts of the 
person: KANGU 'belly', NGUH 'intestines' and MO 'bones'; and one compound is formed 
with the abstract attribute of the person MEN 'ideas'. The presence of NGUH in an 
emotional predicate is unusual, since nguh-no is normally assigned to physiological 
descriptions. The compound may be archaic. In addition to this list, I encountered two 
probably archaic predicates where the second component (not the first; see comments on 
kodj-yirru) relates only etymologically to an attribute of the person or an organ: yirru-beng 
'conflict, anger'+MIND 5 andyirru-kuddu 'conflict, anger'+HEART6, both with the sense 'be 
mean'. 
The compounds formed with these nouns and YIRRU predicates are near-synonyms of the 
YIRRU predicates in question, meaning 'be angry', 'be aggressive' etc.7

This process of specification could explain the relative proliferation of attributes of the 
person and invisible body-parts, in this YIRRU set. Indeed, we saw in Chapter 8 that 
KANGU 'belly1 and some words for 'hearf can stand metonymically for the locus of 
emotions. MO 'bones' may replace KANGU in some of these compounds. As a result, 
KAN GU 'belly' and other invisible parts of the person may also be used to specify the sense 
of yirru 'conflict, anger' as emotional, like MEN 'ideas' does in (5). This analysis provides a 
hypothesis for the existence of the noun kangu-yirru-no and of the frequent KANGU-YIRRU 
alternatives to YIRRU compounds (Chapter 9, 1.1.2, 1.5). Since YIRRU compounds can by 
themselves attract an emotional reading, the contribution of KANGU 'belly' there is partly 
redundant, and thus relatively transparent. 
1.1.2 Summary 
Among the relatively productive [noun+YIRRU predicates] compounds outlined in Table 1, 
two kinds of compounds are found. Where the noun is a visible part of the person, the 
compound is a behavioral hyponym of the original predicate, with the body-part 
contributing semantic specification (literal or metonymic). Where the noun is not visible­
an invisible body-part or an abstract attribute of the person-the compounds are near­
synonyms of the original predicate. These nouns do not contribute a neat semantic 
modification, but seem to specify the predicates as emotional (while they are originally 
ambiguous between behavior and emotion). That abdominal organs may contribute this 
emotional specification probably results from their role in various emotion metaphors 
(Chapter 8). 
Metaphors and metonymies play a relatively minor role in the [ noun+ YIRRU predicates] 
set. While the metonymy INTERNAL ORGAN FOR EXPERIENCER OF EMOTIONS, matching emotion 
metaphors, is indeed a key to the emotional connotations of invisible body-parts, the set 
instantiates very few other conceptual tropes. 8

As in the YIRRU 'conflict, anger' set, with several compounds, the specification is 
determined by the connotations of the added body-part. Mumu-yer(mu) 'eyes'+'avoid 
interaction for fear of others' means 'avoid visual interaction with potential lover' rather 
than just 'avoid visual interaction' (which is koh-yer(mu), 'eyes/gaze'+'avoid interaction 
for fear of others') . This is consistent with the fact that as is cross-linguistically common, 
MUMU 'eyes' is used metonymically in compounds denoting sexual desire ( e.g. mumu-nan 
'look at someone with sexual desire', since sexual desire involves watching the desired 
person intensely , and making eye contact, see 2.1).9 
Likewise, berru-yer(mu) 'chest'+'avoid interaction for fear of others' means 'avoid social 
interactions (with taboo kin)', drawing from the metonymic occurrence of BERRU (or its 
allomorph BERR) in various compounds denoting social interactions. These can refer to 
friendly, 'joking' 10 social interactions ( e.g. berr-wan, 'chest'+ 'follow/ come close', 'interact 
nicely with someone', and berr-burrama, 'chest' +'good, healthy', 'a funny story'), or on the 
contrary, to taboo social interactions, like with berru-yer(mu). Unsurprisingly, BERRU 
'chest' is used in posture and orientation compound predicates, for instance berru-di 
'chest' +'stand/be', 'face towards', [BERRU+cardinal point] 'face towards cardinal point', 
etc. Facing someone is usually a condition for interacting socially with them. In the 
Dalabon context, this aspect of social interactions is highlighted by taboo practices, 
whereby people in a taboo relationship should avoid facing each other-but may talk to 
some extent, as long as the interaction remains physically distant. In this avoidance 
strategy, facing each other is in focus: it is the aspect of social interaction to be avoided. 
This correlates with the linguistic salience of the FACING SOMEONE FOR SOCIALLY INTERACTING 
WITH SOMEONE metonymy, at play with BERRU 'chest' compounds. These taboo rules also 
explain why berru-yer(mu) 'chest' +'avoid interaction for fear of others', 'avoid social 
interactions', is frequently used to describe someone avoiding interactions with taboo kin.

1.2.3 Dolku-yer(mu) 'back'+'avoid interactions for fear of others' 
Dolku-yer(mu) 'back' +'avoid interaction for fear of others', 'scared in strange 
surroundings/feel the presence of someone behind', is neither a synonym nor a hyponym 
of yer(mu). As illustrated by (9), dolku-yer(mu) 'back' +'avoid interaction for fear of others' 
is often used to describe someone feeling uncomfortable in strange surroundings, and 
wary of potential attacks from behind (whether buffaloes, spirits, enemies ... ). On one 
occasion, it was used to describe someone feeling the presence of a non-threatening 
person in their back.

1.3 Dje-bruH(mu) 'be sulky, be sad/put on a dark face' 
1.3.1 Sense and etymology 
Dje-bruH(mu), literally 'nose/nostrils/face'+'blow', has three distinct senses. The most 
frequent sense, which is also the most accessible to speakers' metalinguistic awareness, is 
both emotional and behavioral: 'be sulky' (10). There is also an emotional sense 'be sad' 
(11 and 12), and a purely behavioral sense 'put on a dark face, a grimace' ((13) contrasting 
with (12)).13

In synchrony, dje-bruH(mu) 'nose/nostril/face'+'blow', 'sulky, sad/put on a dark face'

in Chapter 8 because it does not motivate a significant number of compound predicates (it

They do not analyze or comment upon the literal reading of dje-bruH(mu), it does not 
show up in Kriol translations, etc. The sentence 'kah-dje-bruhmu' was accepted as a 
description of a buffalo blowing in anger (presumably 'it is blowing from the nose'), but 
the speaker established no correlation with the lexicalized compound meaning 'sulky, 
sad/put on a dark face'.

The language of emotions in Dalabon 
It is likely that the compound dje-bruH[mu) originated in a different metaphor. While 
bruH[mu) commonly means 'blow' in synchrony, there exists an isolated and probably 
archaic use where bruH[mu) means for a pregnant women to 'grow'. A cognate is found in 
Jawoyn, with the sense 'swell up' (bur'-ma-, [bu17ma]).16 Thus, an etymon of bruH[mu) 
probably had the sense 'swell up' (possibly in conjunction with the sense 'blow'). This is 
supported by the existence of Kriol shwelopnos (Eng. 'swell up' +'nose'), 'be sulky, angry'. 
Furthermore, emotion terms relating to sulking and anger, and meaning literally 'big nose' 
are reported in in other parts of the continent ( e.g. Central Australia (Kaytetye, Turpin 
(2002:281), Western Desert (Kukatja, (Peile 1997:128)), suggesting possible sources for 
Kriol shwelopnos. Finally, association of swelling with hostile feelings (particularly anger) 
are cross-linguistically common-a possible extension of the ANGER IS PRESSURE IN A 
CONTAINER and BODY AS A CONTAINER OF ANGER metaphors. Yet in Dalabon, the sense 'grow' of 
bruH[mu) is no longer productive in synchrony: speakers understand the verb as meaning 
'blow'. As a result, dje-bruH[mu) could only be interpreted literally as 'blowing from the 
nose', and the resulting metaphors are not cognitively active. 
1.3.2 Body-part alternations 
While the metaphor that presumably motivated dje-bruH[mu) 'nose/nostril/face' +'blow', 
'sulky, sad/put on a dark face' is no longer accessible to speakers' metalinguistic 
awareness in synchrony, they still take into account the compositionality of the compound. 
Speakers identified DJE as the nose or the face, for instance translating the compound as 
'salkibala nos' or 'salkibalafeis en nos': 'sulky nose', 'sulky face and nose', in Kriol. 
As with YIRRU 'conflict, anger' predicates andyer[mu) 'avoid interaction for fear of others', 
a (smaller) number of [visible body-part+BRUH(MU)] compounds were encountered. DJE 
'nose/nostril/face' was replaced by another body-part, clearly matching the part involved 
in the emotional behavior described, as listed in Table 3.17 The main structuring principle 
of the set is the same as in the YIRRU 'conflict, anger' and yer[mu) 'avoid interactions for 
fear of others' sets: alternating body-parts yields hyponyms, specifying which body-part is 
involved in the emotional behavior in question.

17 Enfield (2001) reports a similar phenomenon in Lao, where facial expressions are described by 
means of descriptions of the parts of the face rather than by means of descriptions of the whole 
face.

Dje-bruH(mu) 'sulky, sad/put on a dark face' is significantly more frequent than these

is that in these two sets, the 'base' predicates are already emotional behavior predicates. 
With the [body-part+BRUH(MU)] set, the 'base' predicate is not an emotional behavior 
predicate, and does not relate to emotions at all, since bruH(mu) means 'blow'. It only 
endorses an emotional behavior sense in [body-part+ BRUH(MU)] constructions.

The language of emotions in Dalabon 
While these compounds occurred spontaneously, they were not always acknowledged in 
elicitation, hence I consider them lexicalized compounds. Rather, speakers seemed to 
create them in response to appropriate contexts, based on a formal analogy with dje­
bruH(mu). In this process, the predicate BRUH(MU), which means 'blow' in isolation, 
licenses an emotional behavior sense in [body-part+ BRUH(MU)] constructions-the 
construction carries part of the emotional sense. This semantic shift is made possible by 
the fact that dje-bruH(mu) 'sulky, sad/put on a dark face' is a compound which presumably 
originated in a metaphor of the type FACIAL EXPRESSION OF EMOTION FOR EMOTION (EFFECT FOR 
CAUSE), a metaphor which is no longer accessible to speakers' metalinguistic awareness. As 
a result, speakers use a [body-part+predicate] emotional behavior compound which they 
can analyze formally, albeit not semantically. On this basis, the sense of the compounds 
can be reanalyzed, and BRUH(MU) is invested with an emotional sense which then 
surfaces in other compounds. 
In line with the patterns of [body-part+emotional behavior predicate] alternations 
described in 1.1 for YIRRU 'conflict, anger' predicates and 1.2 for yer(mu) 'avoid 
interactions for fear of others', speakers alternate the body-part combined with 
BRUH(MU) 'blow /QUIET' to specify which body-part is involved in the emotional 
behavior, thus producing a set of [body-part+BRUH(MU)] emotional predicates where the 
emotional behavior sense is conveyed by the construction. This process of alternation is 
based on formal analogy with other sets of compounds discussed above. While an eroded 
metaphor is at the origin of the base-predicate dje-bruH(mu) 'nose/nostril/face' +'blow', 
'sulky, sad/put on a dark face', the other compounds in the set result from formal 
analogies with other sets and yield compositional interpretations. In synchrony, this 
mechanism of compound formation has little to do with metaphors. 
1.4 BRUK 'dry/QUIET' 
The adjective bruk 'dry' also occurs throughout a set of emotional compound predicates 
with alternating nouns. Bruk does not denote either an emotion or an emotional behavior; 
[noun+BRUK] predicates denote lack of agitation-whether emotional or behavioral. As 
suggested in Chapter 9 (3.2), the connection of bruk 'dry' with lack of agitation is most 
probably rooted in a metaphor of the type COMPOSURE IS DRYNESS, or maybe more 
specifically, EMOTIONAL COMPOSURE IS DRYNESS. This metaphor derives naturally from the

The set is relatively coherent semantically. All its behavioral members have to do with the 
absence of (usually negative) activity, 1s and all its emotional members have to do with the 
absence of negative emotion, i.e. absence of emotional agitation. With body-part nouns, the 
agitation is often behavioral, its nature being specified either with reference to the 
function of the part in question (dalu-bruk 'mouth'+'dry', 'not speak', (14), analogous to 
dalu-yer{mu) 'mouth' +'avoid interactions for fear of others', 'be too shy to talk', 1.2), or 
with reference to a connotation of the body-part acquired via a metonymy. This occurs 
with MUD 'body hair1, metonymically associated with fear via goosebumps, a physiological 
response to fear (where the resulting compound is thus emotional); 19 and with MUMU 
'eyes', metonymically associated with sexual desire (which involves watching the desired 
person intensely, and making eye contact) (15).

[Visible body-part+BRUK] behavioral compounds imply metaphors consistent with the 
EMOTIONAL COMPOSURE IS DRYNESS metaphor, namely the more general COMPOSURE IS DRYNESS 
and the more specific IDLE BODY-PART IS DRY BODY-PART.20 
1.4.1.1 Metaphors and formal analogy 
It is indisputable that in synchrony, a metaphor COMPOSURE IS DRYNESS is detectable in the 
BRUK set. Historically, such a metaphor is most probably at the origin of at least one of the 
compounds in the set. Since emotional compounds are more numerous and more common 
than behavioral metaphors, the original metaphor may be an emotional metaphor such as 
EMOTIONAL COMPOSURE IS DRYNESS, EMOTIONS ARE FLUIDS being cross-linguistically common. 
Whil,e this is the best explanation for the initial association of bruk 'dry' with the absence 
of emotional or behavioral agitation, the role of metaphor with respect to the formation of 
further BRUK compounds is less clear. The justification for postulating conceptual 
metaphors as the historical motivation of linguistic forms is when only such conceptual 
metaphors may explain a particular constellation of forms (Lakoff & Johnson 1980; Lakoff 
1987; Kovecses 2002). However, here, there exists a competing explanation. Since the 
BRUK set is structurally analogous to several other sets, there are reasons to think that the 
semi-productivity of the set is not channelled by the COMPOSURE IS DRYNESS metaphor, but 
by formal analogy. 
The BRUK set is very similar to the dje-bruH[mu) 'nose/nostrils/face'+'blow' 'sulky, 
sad/put on a dark face' set: body-part nouns combine with a non-emotional predicate, on 
the basis of a [body-part+non-emotional predicate] compound endorsed with an 
emotional sense motivated by a (frozen) metaphor. There are no reasons to see metaphor 
as a better historical explanation for the existence and configuration of the set than formal 
analogy with other semi-compositional sets. In addition, there are no signs-translations, 
free or intended metaphors etc.-that this dryness metaphor is cognitively salient for 
speakers in synchrony. If the explanation by formal analogy is correct, it makes sense to 
say that BRUK in [noun+BRUK] compounds conveys the sense 'lacking agitation', rather 
than the sense 'dry' and its metaphorical implications-just like BRUH(MU) conveys the 
20 As discussed in Chapter 9 (Section 2), the only compound formed with a generic noun, wadda­
bruk 'home' +
1 
dry', 'quiet, focused', does not yield very clear metaphors. 
,..., 381,..., 
[PDF PAGE 407]
The language of emotions in Dalabon 
sense 'sulky' rather than 'blow' in [body-part+BRUH(MU)] compounds. The emotional 
sense of BRUK is tied to the construction. 
This question of whether the BRUK set is motivated by a metaphor or by formal analogy is 
partly idle, because it is not clear which kind of evidence could, in this case, discriminate 
strictly between the two hypotheses. The question is nonetheless worth raising, in my 
view, because each hypothesis suggests a different path of semantic change, with different 
roles for body-parts, metaphors and strictly linguistic mechanisms. If metaphor motivates 
the whole set, we postulate that speakers exploit the conceptual, figurative potential of 
body-parts and other concrete aspects of the world to create new lexical forms and assign 
meanings to them. If formal analogy is at play, we postulate that speakers expand formal 
and semantic regularities that exist in their language to create new forms and assign 
meanings to them. With the latter hypothesis, the linguistic structure has a much stronger 
role in determining linguistic representations. Linguistic rules may then suggest 
conceptual metaphors (rather than being triggered by conceptual metaphors), which 
speakers may, in turn, choose to take into account or not. If metaphor is the driving 
principle, conceptual representations determine linguistic forms; if formal analogy is the 
driving principle, linguistic rules and forms may determine or inspire linguistic and 
conceptual representations. 21 As mentioned above, I have not observed that Dalabon 
speakers exploit COMPOSURE IS DRYNESS metaphors, but this is in theory possible. 22 
. 1.5 Behavioral predicates 
The base-predicates of the three sets presented in previous sections are emotional 
behavior predicates, i.e. predicates that denote a type of behavior and its emotional trigger 
(as defined in Chapter 1, 1.2.2.3). In contrast, the Dalabon verbs redji 'smile, laugh' and run 
'cry' are strictly behavioral. While smiling/laughing is often associated with being pleased, 
21 The same could apply to BRUH(MU) 'blow' compounds, although the set is much more restricted,

22 The interplay between metaphor and derivation, as two different mechanisms oflexical creation, 
has been explored by Goatly (1997 /2011:Chapter 3). Goatly acknowledges important interactions

for metaphorical extensions and transfers of meaning' (1997/2011: 106). According to Goatly,· 
derivations (including compounds) are more likely to attract more new metaphorical senses than 
other lexical items. Like Goatly, I emphasize interactions between derivation and metaphors, but 
my suggestion is different. I hypothesize that compounds (which are derivations) can suggest new 
conceptual metaphors , based on their compositional meaning . The process does not involve 
assigning a new sense to the compound , but simply reinterpreting it as a metaphor.

1.5.1.1 Emotional compounds with redji 'smile, laugh' 
In contrast with facial body-parts, YOLH 'pep, feelings' contributed an important semantic 
shift: as shown in (21), the relatively frequentyolh-redji denotes an emotional state, 'being 
cheerful, happy', rather than a behavior. The less frequent kangu-redji 'belly' +'smile, laugh' 
took a similar sense. Both were used in particular in a context where someone had to hide 
their being pleased, thus contrasting visible and invisible aspects of the person.

1. 6 Conclusions on emotional behavior sets 
None of the five sets of emotional behavior predicate compounds described above present 
the exact same structure, but they do display family resemblances. Several sets are 
structured around a compositional or semi-compositional core of compounds, where 
visible body-parts specify which part of the experiencer is involved in an emotional 
behavior. In several sets, invisible body-part nouns and abstract-attribute nouns specify 
predicates as emotional, as opposed to behavioral. A number of body-part and abstract­
attribute nouns recur through several sets. Many of them contribute a semantic 
specification resulting from their denotation or from the function of the body-part in 
question. With other body-parts, the semantic contribution relies upon tropes, mostly 
metonymies, and is systematized by regular association of the body-part with a particular 
emotional connotation throughout a number of predicate sets. The following section 
discusses these connotations. 
2. Body-parts with emotional connotations 
The body-part nouns which contribute semantically to emotional behavior compounds on 
the basis of a trope are listed in Table 7, which also lists abstract attributes of the person 
nouns which can specify a given compound as emotional.26 
Apart from NJERRH '(potentially dead) body', all body-parts have clear connotations. 
Compounds with NJERRH '( dead) body' were marginal and the contribution of NJERRH is 
not entirely clear, but it seems to convey intensification:

2.1 EFFECT FOR CAUSE metonymies 
Some of the nouns listed in Table 7 occur in very large sets of predicates structured 
around metaphors. This is the case with KANGU 'belly', NGURLK 'HEART' and YOLH 
'feelings', described in extenso in Chapter 8. Others rely upon a more isolated metonymy, 
and then spread through (shorter) sets which do lend themselves to metaphorical 
interpretation. As in many languages (Kovecses 1990:75), MUD 'body hair' connects with 
fear via goosebumps reactions (PHYSICAL REACTION FOR EMOTION, BODY-PART INVOLVED IN 
PHYSICAL REACTION FOR PHYSICAL REACTION, EFFECT FOR CAUSE). MUMU 'eyes', connects with 
·1 
sexual desire because this emotional state leads to intense observation and eye contact 
(RESULTING BEHAVIOR FROM EMOTIONAL CAUSE, EFFECT FOR CAUSE). In the Dalabon context in 
particular, eye contact from a distance is interpreted as a sexual offer (people say that 
lovers exchange gaze as signals to meet up secretly in the bush). 
The tables below recapitulate the compounds ( emotional and otherwise) where MUMU 
and MUD endorse these connotations. Only two MUD 'body hair' compounds are 
emotional, instantiating metonymies of the type BODY HAIR FOR EXPERIENCER OF FEAR 
metonymies (plus the EMOTIONAL COMPOSURE IS DRYNESS metaphor), via goosebumps (25). It 
is found with the root KELE, which occurs in Bininj Gun-wok with the sense 'fear', but is 
not an independent Dalabon lexeme. MUD seems to relate to a particular type of fear, such 
as apprehension, fear of a scary environment (26). It was not found in contexts ·were fear 
relates to a clearly identified and immediate threat (non-metaphorical DJONG compounds 
are preferred in such cases (see Chapter 6, 3.4)).

While KANGU 'belly' compounds have developed an extensive network of emotion 
metaphors, MUD 'body hair' and MUMU 'eyes' only instantiate a couple. In the case of 
KANGU compounds, metaphors constitute the most convincing (and sometimes the only) 
explanation for the existence of some compounds, but with MUD 'body hair' and MUMU 
'eyes', formal analogies between sets of emotional behavior compounds may explain some 
compounds more convincingly. 
For instance, mumu-yer{mu) 'eyes' +'avoid interactions for fear of others' was used to 
describe women avoiding eye contact with potential lovers. This compound follows the 
compositionality principle at play in the yer{mu) set: the body-part in question is involved 
in avoidance behavior, a recurring contribution of body-parts throughout the set. This is 
also in line with the shared representations whereby sexual desire is associated with eye 
contact, and thus constitutes a bridging context where the behavior involving the eyes, and 
the behavior triggering the metonymy are aligned. With mumu-bruk 'eyes'+'dry/QUIET' 
'not flirt', the role of the eyes in a specific behavior is backgrounded, because 'not flirt' is 
more general than 'not make eye contact'. Therefore, MUMU connotes 'sexual desires' 
more directly (independent of the body-part), so that the connotation is reinforced . 
However, the metaphor DRYNESS OF THE EYES FOR ABSENCE OF SEXUALLY DRIVEN BEHAVIOR is far­
fetched, does not occur elsewhere in the language, and is not salient for speakers. It seems 
unlikely that this metaphor is responsible for the production of mumu-bruk, and thus for 
the reinforcement of the 'sexual desire' connotation of MUMU 'eyes'. Rather, the 
compound results from formal analogy with other sets, and in particular with djong-bruk

2.2 PART FOR WHOLE metonymies 
2.2.1 KODJ 'crown of head/head' and the social actor 
KODJ, which primarily means 'crown of head', and 'head' by extension, stands, among 
other things, 29 for the social individual-a relatively natural metonymy (PART FOR WHOLE, 
PHYSICAL ACTOR FOR SOCIAL ACTOR). KODJ is found in compounds denoting interactions of 
29 In cognitive compound predicates, KODJ represents the locus of intellectual processes and 
knowledge (Ponsonnet 2009a:21-23), based on a cross-linguistically common metonymy whereby 
the crown of the head stands for the brain ( CONTAINER IS CONTENT), and the metaphor THE BRAIN IS THE 
INSTRUMENT OF INTELLECTION. 
,...,, 3 9 3 ,...,, 
[PDF PAGE 419]
The language of emotions in Dalabon 
individuals as social actors in a social network ( e.g. kodj-nganj-mang 'crown of 
head/head'+ ?+get', 'share according to social etiquette'-for instance the meat of a 
kangaroo). It is also found in various compounds relating to conjugal relationships, a 
special case of social context. In addition, KODJ 'crown of head/head' occurs in compounds 
relating to babies to be born (kodj-nga/ka 'head' +'find', 'beget a child'). Kodj-no denotes the 
crown of the head. The crown of the head of the child is the first part of the person 
appearing at birth, which could stand for the person. Irrespective of this hypothesis the 
cluster of connotations (social actor, conjugal actor, expected baby) can be explained in 
the following way. 
The Dalabon social context can be described as a saturated social network, where each 
individual stands as a node. Begetting a child is adding a node to the . network. 
Furthermore, in pre-colonial times, this social network was a guide to conjugal unions. 
One would marry with the right node ( as defined in terms of kin relations and patrilineal 
descent lines) in order to maintain balance in the network (Hiatt 1968; Keen 1982). In the 
Dalabon context, the 'right node' did not always exist, due to relatively low demographics. 
For this reason, newborn babies could be promised as spouses before birth, because of 
people awaiting spouses. In the social network, each individual, and also each newborn 
baby, was defined as someone's potential spouse. This system could explain the 
extension/specialization of the connotation of KODJ from the social-actor (an expected 
metonymy) to the actor-in-conjugal-relationships metonymy, and also to babies to be 
born. 
The KODJ 'crown of head/head' set (Table 10) is larger than the MUD 'body hair' and 
MUMU 'eyes' set, and does instantiate more specific, and relatively diverse metaphors, 
such as resistance (kodj-murduk 'head' +'hard/strong\ 'emotionally closed'), destruction 
(kodj-dadj(mu) 'head'+'be cut, end', 'become upset and interrupt social interactions'), and 
blockage (kodj-dukkan 'head'+'tie up', 'be upset with').

With all the predicates falling under this metonymy, the net contribution of KANGU to the

This matches the contribution of KANGU in the emotional behavior set described above, 
where KANGU specifies the event as emotional: kangu-run 'belly'+'cry', 'feel sad (because 
of separation)', kangu-redji 'belly' +'smile, laugh', 'be pleased', etc. The nature of the 
emotional input of KANGU in the compounds of Table 12 varies. With behavioral 
predicates ( e.g. run 'cry' and redji 'smile, laugh'), KAN GU imposes an emotional reading 
where there is none originally. With 'generic' predicates, which can apply to the whole 
person (e.g. burrama 'good, healthy', see Chapter 8, 1.4.2.1), KANGU narrows down the 
application of the predicate to the person's emotions. With emotional behavior words, 
which combine a behavioral and an emotional sense ( e.g. yirru 'conflict, anger'), KAN GU 
seems to specify the sense as emotional, ruling out an otherwise possible behavioral 
interpretation. With emotional predicates, KANGU does not seem to make a semantic 
contribution (not even intensity), but simply emphasizes the emotional nature of the 
event. 
Thus, while the analysis of KANGU compounds in terms of metaphors and metonymies is 
valuable 1 the same compounds may also be considered from a different angle. Various 
KANGU compounds also belong to other, so to speak perpendicular sets, where KANGU 
alternates with other body-parts while the predicate remains the same. When contrasted 
with the other members of these [variable noun+fixed predicate] sets, KANGU simply 
means 'emotional(ly)'. The input of KANGU may be analyzed as a regular semantic 
contribution, and the predicates may be interpreted compositionally. As a result 1 from a 
diachronic point of view, conceptual metaphors may have played no role at all in the

compositional compounds, with KANGU meaning 'emotional, emotionally', a sense 
acquired from repeated contrasts within various semi-productive and semi-regular sets

It was shown in Chapter 8 that speakers perceive belly metaphors and exploit them in

judging by their reactions when exposed to presumably 'new' KAN GU compounds, which 
they tend to interpret as emotional. While this interpretation competes with metaphorical 
interpretation, it seems very plausible that speakers' can perceive both aspects ( either 
that different speakers adopt different views, or that one speaker may adopt different 
views at different times). 
3. Analogy, compositionality, body-parts and emotions 
Dalabon has a number of semi-productive, semi-compositional sets of [animate-part 
noun+predicate] compounds, where the base predicates and the resulting compounds 
relate to emotional behaviors . Chapters 8 and 9 presented [noun+predicate] sets where 
tropes such as metonymy and metaphor play a structuring role-and may therefore be 
regarded as probable historical moti vations for the sets. The sets described in this chapter 
. do call upon various metonymies which confer some connotations to some body-parts. Yet 
the structuring principles across these sets are not conceptual but formal: namely ( semi-) 
compositionality and formal analogy between sets. 
I have described six semi-productive sets of such [animate-part noun+emotional behavior] 
predicates. While each set displays a slightly different structure, the sets present recurring 
family resemblances. A significant proportion of the compounds in these sets attract 
(semi-)compositional interpretations: when the noun component is a visible body-part, 
most of the time it specifies the nature of the behavior as involving this body-part. Some 
compounds exploit metonymies whereby a given body-part is associated with a given 
emotion or context ( e.g. MUD 'body hair' and fear, KODJ 'crown of head/head' and 
social/conjugal relation). These metonymies also recur, and develop, across the sets. 
31 Regarding the importance of perceiving compositionality in collocations, see Schroten (2000). 
"" 4 0 0 "" 
[PDF PAGE 426]
Chapter 10 • Body-parts and emotional behaviors 
However, these metonymies are backgrounded in the emotional behavior sets, in the 
sense that they are not a driving principle of lexical production. Instead, compositionality 
and formal analogy between sets play a structuring role. 
While the matter is different, these semi-productive sets bear some resemblances to what 
Burenhult & Levinson (2009) call 'semplates
1
• Semplates (a portmanteau for semantic 
templates) are conceptual patterns (templates) that, within a language, underlie several 
lexical sets which are not necessarily related morphologically. For instance, in Tzeltal, 
directions, relational nouns (boundaries, edges etc.), and motion verbs are 
morphologically unrelated, but they all follow the same conceptual pattern of 
representation of space, because they all draw similar conceptual distinctions. Dalabon 
emotional behavior sets do not display such a clear and regular template as the ones 
Burenhult & Levinson call 'semplates'. In addition, given the topic, it would be difficult to 
articulate clear-cut conceptual distinctions such as the ones found in space (where up, 
down, across etc. provide relatively straightforward etic grids). However, emotional 
behavior predicates do display family resemblances in forms and concepts, and present 
recurrent non-metaphorically grounded conceptual associations, weaving a conceptual 
and linguistic template for lexical sets of emotional behavior compounds, and thus fo r the 
conceptual representation of emotional behaviors. 
While the core of the (semi-)compositional compounds in each set relates to body-parts , 
the sets are not limited to body-part specification, i.e. to the specification of visible aspects 
of emotional events. We also find [animate-part noun+emotional behavior predicate] 
compounds, where the invisible/abstract noun imposes an emotional reading to the 
predicate. Metaphors and metonymies play a role in the original conceptual association 
between these invisible body-parts (KANGU 'belly' in particular) and emotional states , but 
compositional principles are also at play. Through repeated contrasts with other members 
of such sets, the morpheme KANGU for instance, which also means 'belly', behaves as if it 
had acquired the sense 'emotional'. In general, in emotional behavior compounds, invisible 
parts of the person also contribute the sense 'emotional'. Speakers seem to endorse such 
compositional interpretations, but this does not prevent them from also endorsing 
metaphorical interpretations. 
Also based on formal analogy and recurring semantic contrasts, predicates having nothing 
to do with the emotional domain may acquire an emotional sense via [animate-part 
,-.; 4 0 1 ,-.; 
[PDF PAGE 427]
The language of emotions in Dalabon 
noun+predicate] constructions. This is the case with BRUH(MU) 'blow', which conveys the 
meaning 'be or look sulky' in emotional compounds, and BRUK 'dry', which conveys the 
feature 'not agitated'. While the presence of these predicates in emotion-related 
compounds is originally motivated by metaphors, the extension of the BRUH(MU) and 
BRUK set seems to be motivated by formal and semantic analogy with other emotional 
behavior sets. Yet these sets may suggest conceptual metaphors to speakers, who may 
choose to exploit them cognitively or not. If this is the case, the respective roles of 
conceptual metaphors and linguistic forms are inverted: linguistic forms motivate 
conceptual metaphors, rather than the reverse. Thus, emotional compounds may not only 
be independent of metaphors: they may actually influence them in some cases. 
Such mechanisms bear some resemblances to semantic reanalysis ( or 'folk etymologies') 
based on homophony (e.g. the French decrepi 'having lost pebbledash' decrepit 'worn out', 
usually conflated by French speakers (see Saussure 1916/1955:121)) or on phonological 
reinterpretations/transformations leading to double etymologies (Rumsey 1983). Yet the 
mechanisms considered here are different, since they do not rely on phonological or 
morphological reanalyzes, but simply on the interplay between various semantic values of 
the same forms, with special affordances created by the [noun+predicate] compound 
structure and family resemblances between sets. 
3.1 Emotional behavior sets and the perception of emotions 
Another question to ask is why such [ animate-part noun+behavior / emotion predicate] 
sets exist in Dalabon. While this is surely not exceptional, not all languages allow speakers 
to be so systematically specific in descriptions of emotional behaviors (in English or 
French, or other Romance languages, there are no words or compounds encapsulating the 
idea that one is 'laughing from the eyes, the nose' etc.). In my data, the tendency is 
probably exaggerated due to the use of visual stimuli, and indeed they were more common 
in descriptions of videos or still pictures, where speakers may feel that they are expected 
to produce thorough bodily descriptions. Yet such visual stimuli are relatively natural in 
this respect (not being very different from watching someone with attention). The 
occurrence of body-part specifications in emotional (and therefore, non-technical) 
utterances related to Rabbit-Proof Fence (26) indicates that specification is indeed 
frequent. Turpin (2002) also notes a propensity to describe emotional behavior in 
Kaytetye. Does it correlate with more intense attention dedicated to the role of the body .in 
,..., 402,..., 
[PDF PAGE 428]

emotional (and social) behaviors? Enfield (2001), who reports a comparable phenomenon 
in Lao, where facial expressions are described by means of descriptions of parts of the face 
rather than as a whole, suggests that such a partition may impact on the way people 
interpret facial expressions _(2001:162-163). Are Dalabon speakers particularly attentive 
to how parts of the body, as opposed to the body as a whole, betray/ express emotions? 
Are they particularly prone to thorough body descriptions? 
This question cannot be answered on the sole basis of ethnographic observation and 
linguistic data: such cognitive orientations should be explored by means of experimental 
protocols. However, a couple of observations are in order. The compositional compounds 
in the emotion behavior sets are standard noun incorporation constructions. Their 
existence is conditioned by the grammatical possibility of incorporating nouns for parts of 
animates, a mechanism which facilitates the specification of which body-part is involved in 
a given event. For some semantic roles, it seems that such a specification is quasi­
compulsory. This is the case with experiencers of affects. Verbs meaning 'ache' are usually 
accompanied by a body-part specifying the locus of the event. If the pain is diffused 
throughout the whole body, MO 'bones' may be used: ngah-mo-ngarrkmu 'I ache all over'. 
On the other hand, the frequency of such body-part specification matches contextual 
relevance: ngarrk(mu) 'ache' alone occurs in contexts where the nature of one's affect-as 
opposed to its location-is in question (is it pain or something el~e?):

With emotional behaviors (and social behaviors 34), on the other hand, body-part 
specification is relatively frequent. 35 In her article on the use of body-parts in emotional 
constructions in Kaytetye, Turpin (2002) observes that in this language some emotions 
are primarily described by means of physical descriptions. Inspired by Peile (1997) and 
Myers (1986) , she suggests that this may be explained by 'a tendency to refer indirectly to 
emotional experience, [maybe] because people are more inclined to talk about things that 
can be perceived externally, rather than speculate on another person's internal feelings'. 
This hypothesis is not confirmed for Dalabon. As Turpin indicates for Kaytetye, in Dalabon 
body-part specification does not apply to any emotions indiscriminately, but targets 
emotions closely associated with a behavior. With other emotions, there exist numerous 
terms referring directly to the cognitive states (see chapters 5 and 6). In addition, I find 
Dalabon speakers relatively prompt to speculate on other people's internal states: 
reported speech-a common narrative technique in Dalabon (Chapter 4, 2.2)-provides 
examples of such speculations, where speakers' accounts of what another person thinks 
can be extensive and detailed. 
The question of the specification of body-parts in emotional events is tackled by Huang 
(2002) about Tsou (Austronesian, Taiwan) . Tsou also offers the possibility of specifying 
which body-part is involved in an emotional behavior, by means of a prefix on the 
behavioral predicate. The phenomena bear some resemblance _ to the one observed in 
Dalabon. Huang argues that the availability, in Tsou, of a grammatical prefixation strategy 
(specifying which body-part is involved in an emotional behavior) generates a cognitive 
pattern whereby Tsou speakers perceive events as 'macro-events' (Talmy 2000:vol. 2 213-
221) involving emotions and behaviors, which in turn results in the absence of tropes 
(metaphors or metonymies) in the emotion lexicon (Huang 2002:177). In contrast, in 
34 Social behavior predicates cannot be discussed in details here to conserve space. Some of them 
involve body-parts like BERRU 'chest' (1.2, 2.1) or REDJ 'side' because they describe behavior by 
means of metonymies involving postures. With some others, no posture is involved but the body­
part specification partakes in a lexicalized [body-part+predicate] construction yielding a social 
sense. This is the case with body-part+ngun 'eat' predicates for instance, which mean 'I thank you'. 
The default body-part is DJE 'nose/nostrils/face': djah-dje-ngunj 'I thank you', literally 'I ate your 
nose'. But DJE can be replaced by MILH 'forehead', yielding the same sense, or by other body-parts 
which specify which part of the thanked person was involved in the event attracting gratitude: djah­
langu-ngunj 'I thank you [for passing me the bottle of water with your hand]', literally 'I ate your 
hand'.

The language of emotions in Dalabon 
Dalabon, the grammatical possibility of specifying which body-part is involved in an 
emotional event by means of noun incorporation does not exclude any strategy of lexical 
creation. Conceptual tropes, derivation following principles of compositionality, and 
formal analogy are all at play in the extension of the lexicon. There is no reason to 
hypothesize a broad 'cognitive pattern' of perception of events as macro-events. Rather, 
some events are perceived as emotional behavior events, in which case body-part 
specification is common, and other events are perceived as strictly emotional, yielding 
metonymies and metaphors. 
My best hypothesis for the frequency of body-part specification with emotional behaviors 
has to do with material culture, and specifically the settings of daily life in pre-colonial 
times (Kovecses 2005:239). Dalabon people (like most Australian peoples in the northern 
part of the continent) often lived in camps, usually grouped under open shelters scattered 
across small areas. Being able to observe each other, from a distance, between groups, 
would have been an important social parameter. This context is perpetuated today: in 
Dalabon communities, people tend to live in front of their houses, rather than inside. 
People of all ages usually keep an eye on what is happening outside, on the road and 
around other houses, and comment upon it. Thorough descriptions of bodily behaviors 
and postures would be relevant to the descriptions and understanding of a given situation, 
where people's behaviors are being observed from a distance, and voices may not be 
audible. In Dalabon, body-part noun incorporation probably favors body-part specification 
by making it a smooth linguistic process. 
4. Conclusions 
While it was demonstrated In previous chapters that body-parts are involved in a 
significant number of Dalabon emotion metaphors and metonymies, the present chapter 
showed that the presence of body-parts in descriptions of emotions is not determined 
uniquely by conceptual tropes. Indeed, body-parts are an important feature in sets of 
emotion-related behavioral predicates, where they specify which part of the experiencer is 
involved in an emotional behavior. Throughout these sets, various body-parts and a couple 
of predicates gain emotional connotations, and invisible body-parts, KANGU 'belly' In 
particular, may be interpreted as meaning 'emotional'. 
,..., 4 0 6 ,..., 
[PDF PAGE 432]
Chapter 10 • Body-parts and emotional behaviors 
These sets are formally and semantically semi-productive, and yield new lexical forms as 
well as semantic shift, largely (albeit not only) under the influence of linguistic 
mechanisms independent of metaphors or metonymies. Among these mechanisms are 
compositionality and formal analogy. These lexical forms are not independent of 
metaphors: they incorporate them, and may also influence them. Some of the lexical forms 
produced via these linguistic mechanisms may, in turn, generate new conceptual 
metaphors. The relation between linguistic forms and conceptual metaphors is inverted: 
linguistic forms may influence conceptual metaphors as well as the reverse. 
Expanding upon the potential influence of linguistic forms and formal principles on 
metaphorical representations of emotions, it is possible to ask whether metaphors may be 
influenced by grammatical features. This hypothesis is tentatively explored in the next and 
last chapter. 
""' 4 0 7 ""' 
[PDF PAGE 433]
11 Excursus: 
The influence of grammar? 
Chapters 7 to 9 explored how some Dalabon emotional compound sets including a body­
part or an attribute of the person are best explained in the light of the conceptual 
metonymies and metaphors which presumably motivated them historically. Chapter 10, 
on the other hand, showed that for a number of sets of compounds of comparable 
structure ([animate-part noun+predicate]), compounds do display some metonymic or 
metaphoric dimension, but other structural principles are primarily at play in their 
formation. The compounds take part in semi-productive sets of compounds where lexical 
production is channelled by compositionality and formal analogy. Thus, they are 
motivated by 'formal' linguistic mechanisms rather than conceptual tropes. It was 
suggested at the end of Chapter 10 that some of these compounds may, however, suggest 
conceptual metaphors, so that the forms in question may motivate conceptual metaphors. 
Thus, in some cases, formal (as opposed to conceptual) principles, and linguistic forms 
themselves, may be the source of conceptual representations, rather than the reverse. 
This final, short chapter expands on this hypothesis of the influence of 'form' on 
conceptual representations. I consider the possibility that some particular grammatical 
features of Dalabon may constrain the type of emotion metaphors used in this language. 
As will be pointed out in Section 1, the discussion is speculative. This chapter does not 
seek to present conclusive arguments, but rather to discuss hypotheses in order to identify 
directions of future research. These hypotheses are articulated in Section 2, which 
explores plausible influences of some grammatical features of Dalabon on emotion 
metaphors. In particular, what metaphors are available for a given emotion or affect seems 
to correlate partly with the nominal subclass of the noun on which these metaphors are 
based. In Dalabon, emotion-related nouns which denote, in synchrony or etymologically, a 
body-part, seem to block representations of emotions as entities independent of the 
person , while other nouns afford them. This correlation is highlighted in 2.1 and 2.2. On 
,..., 4 0 8 ,..., 
[PDF PAGE 434]
Chapter 11 • Excursus: The influence of grammar? 
the other hand, this suggestion does not explain why Dalabon body-based emotion 
metaphors do not afford these independent-entity metaphors, while among the world's 
languages, many body-based emotion metaphors do yield such representations. In 2.3, I 
point to two morphosyntactic properties of the body-part (animate-part) nominal 
subclass, namely quasi-obligatory possessor raising and propensity to incorporate, which 
could possibly explain this channelling of metaphors. Finally, 2.4 explores the fact that 
while non-body-based nouns do trigger metaphorical representations of emotions as 
independent entities, such representations remain marginal in Dalabon even with these 
nouns. Indeed, most metaphors based on these nouns avoid this representation, and I 
suggest that this could result from the Dalabon grammatical preference for experiencer 
subjects. 
The suggestions articulated along this chapter leave many questions unanswered, and 
they are not intended to be conclusive. Along the way, I suggest how they could be further 
elaborated and tested by means of cross-linguistic comparison. 
1. The influence of grammatical features 
on linguistic representations of emotions 
-
Ultimately, hypothesizing an influence of grammar upon metaphors relates to the 
'Whorfian' question of linguistic relativity, since the hypothesis questions the influence of 
linguistic patterns on representations, hence on thought. However, the first step of the 
problem, which I will explore here, does not bear upon the relation between language and 
something external to language (thought or 'culture', see Wharf (1956), Lucy (1992)). 
Instead, the problem is internal to language, since grammatical features (the purported 
constraining factor) and metaphors (linguistic descriptions of emotions) both lie within 
language. 
Not many authors have dealt with the question of how grammatical features influence 
metaphors. The problem is certainly not independent of the general question of the range 
and factors of cultural variations of metaphors, tackled by Kovecses (2005). Kovecses only 
makes a very brief mention of the potential Whorfian effects of metaphors (2005:284), by 
which he means the effect of metaphors on cognition-but the question of the influence of 
grammatical features on metaphors is not considered. Several authors have studied or 
,..., 409,..., 
[PDF PAGE 435]
The language of emotions in Dalabon 
questioned the effects of metaphors on thought or cognition in general, either language 
internally (Reddy 1979 /1993; Schon 1979 /1993) or by means of -experimental protocols 
designed to test cognition independent of language (Boroditsky 2001; Meier & Robinson 
2005; Robinson et al. 2006). Goatly (2007:Chapter 7) discusses correlations between 
metaphorical patterns and thought/ culture, but he considers metaphors deeply 
entrenched in grammar, which correspond to quasi-universal categories-such as 
semantic roles divisions, transitivity for instance. His account rearticulates the analyses of 
Langacker (1991) and Talmy (1988) in terms of metaphors. Goatly does not consider 
specific cases of influence of particular grammatical features on metaphors, but rather 
reconsiders the broad Whorfian question 'can grammar shape worldviews?' in 
metaphorical terms. 1 It is hard to see how these general suggestions could be tested 
against data provided by cross-linguistic comparison. 2 
I have not found, in these works or in works on linguistic relativity (Lucy 1992; Levinson & 
Gumperz 1996; Niemeier & Dirven 2000; Enfield 2002b ), any systematic study of the 
influence of grammatical features on metaphors. Huang (2002) does hypothesize a 
correlation between a grammatical feature of Tsou (Austronesian, Taiwan) and its 
emotion metaphors . The author suggests that the 'grammatical prefixation strategy
1 
(the 
possibility of specifying which body-part is involved in an emotional behavior by means of 
a prefix on the predicate) results in the quasi-absence of metaphors/metonymies for 
emotions in this language . However, according to Huang, the correlation goes via a 
cognitive step. The grammatical features in question lead Tsou speakers to perceive 
events in a certain way, which in turn leads them to avoid metaphors. Hence Huang does 
not hypothesize a direct influence of grammar on metaphors. 3 
1 In addition, he is more interested in the association of metaphors with culture and ideology, not in 
the link between particular patterns of diverse individual languages with metaphors. 
2 Not concerned with metaphors in particular , but with the language of emotions more broadly and 
its relation to grammar , Wierzbicka (1999:262-263) seeks to demonstrate that the particular Polish 
emphasis on the spontaneity of emotions is reflected in Polish grammar. She describes several 
Polish syntactic constructions denoting various degrees of spontaneity of an emotion, and argues 
that this wealth of constructions corresponds to a particular cultural stance on emotions. 
Wierzbicka is not concerned with the question of how grammar may influence language, but rather 
with an 'adirectionaI1 correlation between the two. She does not outline particular mechanisms of 
influence , in one direction or another . 
3 In fact, the question tackled by Huang (2002) is closer to the one raised for Dalabon in Chapter 10, 
i.e. the author tried to shed light upon the tendency to specify which body-part is involved in 
emotion behaviors. My suggestions to explain the same tendency in Dalabon do not match Huang

Chapter 11 • Excursus: The influence of grammar? 
In the following paragraphs, I articulate some suggestions as to how some grammatical 
features of Dalabon could · possibly influence emotion metaphors and the linguistic 
representation of emotions more generally. At this stage, my suggestions are not claims 
but hypotheses, the testing of which lies beyond the scope of this study, but could be 
tackled in future cross-linguistic research. The issue, like most Whorfian-like questions 
concerning the influence of linguistic patterns, is slippery. Lucy (1996:48) lists some often 
neglected methodological requirements for sound research on linguistic relativity. Such 
research should: 
1) be comparative i.e. involve several languages; 
2) deal with a significant language variable such as one or more central grammatical 
categories, rather than a relatively minor vocabulary set; 
3) assess the performance of individual speakers aside from explicitly verbal 
contexts; 
4) preferably, deal with referential categories. 
The hypotheses below focus on relatively central grammatical categories, namely the 
preference of some nominal subclasses for possessor raising, and the preference of some 
verbs for experiencer subjects-hence (2) is fulfilled. Condition (3), and to a lesser extent 
( 4 ), are required in order to establish correlations between linguistic features and 
cognition. Here, hypothetical correlations are language internal ( see above), and therefore 
(3) and (4) do not apply. Condition (1), cross-linguistic comparison, is indispensable. A 
comparative approach remains beyond the scope of this work, but the suggestions 
discussed in Section 2 could indeed be tested against an appropriate sample of languages, 
as suggested throughout the paragraphs . 
I now turn to the exploration of possible correlations between some Dalabon grammatical 
features and Dalabon emotion metaphors. Sections 2.1 and 2.2 discuss the correlation 
between these metaphors and the nominal subclass of the noun they are based upon. 
Section 2.3 suggests how some morphosyntactic properties of these nominal subclasses 
could play a role, as well as other syntactic preferences properties (2.4). 
2. Nominal subclasses properties and emotion metaphors 
It was pointed out in Chapter 8 that Dalabon emotion metaphors usually represent 
emotions as states or parts of the person, and only very rarely as entities independent of 
,..., 411,..., 
[PDF PAGE 437]
The language of emotions in Dalabon 
the person, even less as agents such as forces or opponents. This is in contrast with many 
languages, where emotions are often represented as independent entities, and as forces­
as in English, French and many languages on other continents (see Chapter 8, Section 4). 
In this section, I discuss various grammatical factors which may help explain why this is 
so. Metaphorical representation of emotions as states of the person or parts of the person 
seems natural when emotion metaphors are grounded in somatic metonymies, as 
discussed in Chapter 8. In somatic metonymies, a physical state frequently associated with 
an emotion ( often a physiological trigger of /response to emotions, like an upset stomach, 
higher heart rate, etc.) stands metonymically for the associated emotion, so that this state 
comes to represent the associated emotion. As a result, emotions are represented 
linguistically as states of the person. Because the physical states in question affect 
particular body-parts, these body-parts are treated linguistically as the loci of these 
emotions ( e.g. the belly). Many languages implement another metonymy, by virtue of 
which the body-part that is the locus of the physical state related to the emotion comes to 
stand metonymically for the emotion, with a metonymy BODY-PART FOR EMOTION (for 
instance, heart can mean 'courage' in English, where it is no longer a state of the heart­
like heart rate-but the heart itself which stands for the emotion). 
Indeed, it was shown in Chapter 8 (1.4.2.1) that the Dalabon somatic metonymies may 
lead to metonymies of the type BODY-PART FOR THE PERSON'S EMOTIONS. This metonymy 
occurs in some compounds, for instance where the predicate is generic, like with kangu­
burrama 'belly' +'good, healthy', 'be nice, feel good emotionally'. Being generic, burrama 
can apply to the whole person, meaning that the person is in good health. Literally, kangu­
burrama can be interpreted as a noun incorporation construction meaning 'healthy from 
the belly'. Therefore, 'healthy from the belly' means 'healthy emotionally', which in terms 
of a trope yields a metonymy BELLY FOR THE PERSON'S EMOTIONS. This metonymy could 
trigger the sense of kangu-no to shift from 'belly' to 'emotions'. This is very possibly what 
happened to yolh-no, which means 'pep, feelings' in synchrony, but is most probably 
related etymologically to abdominal body-parts (see Chapter 8, 3.1). In this scenario, 
body-part nouns may acquire an emotional sense via somatic metaphors. However, in 
Dalabon, the emotional noun yolh-no 'pep, feelings' remains linguistically depicted as a 
part of the person. Indeed, yolh-no 'pep, feelings' belongs to the same nominal subclass as 
body-parts and other attributes of the person. Whether incorporated or used externally, 
yolh-no raises its possessor like other body-part nouns do: it is treated linguistically as an 
"' 412 "'

inalienable part of the person. As a result, YOLH compounds cannot represent emotions as 
entities independent of the person, but only as parts or states of the person.

Yirru belongs to the generic nominal subclass, and the treatment ofyirru as a full argument 
inyirru-ngalka is consistent with the morphosyntactic properties of this nominal subclass. 
When used in isolation,yirru primarily denotes events, namely conflicts or angry behavior. 
The emotional sense is backgrounded and becomes foregrounded in compounds. Whether 
in isolation or in compounds, yirru does not denote a body-part, and there is no indication 
that it relates to a body-part etymologically. 7 In line with this disconnection from body­
parts and from the animate-part nominal subclass, YIRRU compound metaphors are not 
grounded in somatic metonymies or other physiological metaphors, and they do 
(marginally) afford representation of an emotion as an entity independent of the person. 
This is in line with the hypothesis that Dalabon representations of emotions as states or 
parts of the person result from the bodily anchorage of these metaphors and from the 
morphosyntactic properties of the associated nominal subclass. However, not all YIRRU 
coin pounds yield EMOTIONS ARE INDEPENDENT ENTITIES metaphors. This is discussed in 2.4.

the origin of the tropes play a part in constraining emotion metaphors. Indeed, neither 
bar-no 'pain' nor yirru 'conflict, anger' relate etymologically to a body-part, and· both are 
represented as entities independent of the person. This correlates with the nominal 
subclass membership of the words in question. Bar-no 'pain' is an inanimate-part noun, 
and yirru 'conflict, anger' is a generic noun. Thus, neither belongs to the subclass of 
inalienable animate-part nouns.

nominal subclass does not explain why body-parts do not shift away from their subclass, 
like they do in many other languages. This is discussed in 2.3, where I suggest that this 
may result from the Dalabon preference for incorporating body-parts and raising their

possessor. Second, the case of yirru 'conflict, anger' is not clear-cut: Dalabon anger

the grammar of Dalabon. 
2.3 Preference for body-parts 
possessor raising and incorporation 
While the hypothetical correlation between body-inspired metaphors and the 
representation of emotions as parts of the person seems to find some grounds within 
Dalabon, it raises obvious difficulties when confronted with other languages. Somatic 
metonymies and other figures involving body-parts as sources and emotions as targets are 
so widespread cross-linguistically that Wierzbicka (1999:36) suggests they are universal. 
Yet in many languages, body-parts do yield BODY-PART FOR EMOTION metonymies where 
emotions are represented as independent entities. Among many other examples, this is the 
case with 'heart' or 'guts' in English (Dirven 1985:108; Niemeier 2000; Geeraerts & 
Gevaert 2008; Goddard 2008; Niemeier 2008), as well as ca:ur ('heart') or tripes ('guts') in 
French, which can all mean 'courage' (as well as 'generosity' for ca:ur). Comparable 
polysemies are found in genetically unrelated languages, for instance Swahili where o-
. mayo translates as 'heart' and 'courage', or Zulu where ibsindi translates as 'liver' and 
'courage' (Dimmendaal 2002). With the French ca:ur 'heart', while the body-part is a count 
noun, ca:ur in the emotional sense is a mass noun ('ii a du ca:ur, 'he's generous', literally 
'he's got heart')8 and no longer a person-part. 
In Dalabon, by contrast, body-parts do not shift away from their nominal subclass. KAN GU 
'belly' and NGERH 'heart/breath', which yield emotion metaphors, behave syntactically 
like other nouns of the animate-part morphosyntactic class: they are incorporable, bound 
nouns, which raise their possessor quasi-systematically when incorporated and when 
used externally. In addition, even when such nouns endorse an abstract, emotional sense, 
like yolh-no 'pep, feelings', they still remain within the same animate-part nominal 
8 This is the default for emotion nouns in French (Krzyzanowska 2009; Novakova & Tutin 2009; 
Goossens 2011). 
,_, 418 ,_, 
[PDF PAGE 444]
Chapter 11 • Excursus: The influence of grammar? 
subclass, with identical morphosyntactic behavior as body-part nouns . For now, the best 
candidate explanations for this are the morphosyntactic constraints bearing on this 
nominal subclass. These constraints could explain why body-parts do not easily evolve 
semantically to represent emotions literally, and why when they do so (like with yolh-no ), 
they are still treated linguistically as parts of the person. Section 2.3.1 considers the 
preference for body-part possessor raising, and 2.3.2 the preference for body-part noun 
incorporation. 
2.3.1 Body-part possessor raising 
In Dalabon (like in Bininj Gun-wok, see Evans (2003:462ff)), body-parts are very 
frequently incorporated and they raise their possessor quasi-systematically, especially 
with verbs of affectedness and when describing bodily processes, i.e. verbs involving an 
experiencer. Hence for intransitive verbs with experiencer subjects (the standard 
argument mapping of emotion predicates, see Chapter 5, 2.2), the subject normally 
remains the person, as evidenced in (9) and . (10) below by the second person prefix dja- (if 
the body-part was referenced on the verb, the prefix would be third person singular ka-). 
The affected body-part is specified as a part of the experiencer, usually by an incorporated 
noun (9), sometimes externally (10). But whether the body-part is incorporated or not, 
with experiencer subjects (i.e. with most body descriptions), affected body-parts very 
rarely stand as an argument of the verb independently of their possessor.

In spite of these marginal possibilities, with verbs denoting affects, bodily processes, 
bodily responses, bodily events, and body descriptions, possessor raising is by far the 
preferred option. As a result, in all these contexts, body-parts are very rarely treated 
syntactically as autonomous arguments, but only as parts of their possessors: it is the 
possessor that attracts overt marking, as person prefixes agree with the possessor, not 
with the part. 
These body-related semantic contexts where possessor raising is strongly preferred are 
precisely the ones which give rise to somatic metonymies (based on bodily processes, 
states etc.) and thus to most emotion metaphors based on body-parts (see Chapter 8). The 
fact that body-parts are only rarely expressed as autonomous arguments, and are instead 
treated syntactically as parts of their possessors in these constructions, may influence the 
ontological status of emotions in metaphors. Since they are not autonomous arguments, 
the body-parts in question, and therefore the emotions they might denote, are not treated 
as metaphorical independent entities. 
Constructions where the body-part which serves as a base to the metonymy /metaphor is 
treated as an argument may favor the emergence of BODY-PART FOR EMOTIONS figures ( e.g. 
HEART FOR COURAGE in English, French and other languages), where the emotion is 
represented linguistically as an entity independent of the person. In Dalabon, in contrast, 
the metonymy BELLY FOR PERSON'S EMOTION occurs (e.g. kangu-burrama 'belly'+'good, 
healthy', 'be nice, feel good emotionally', see Chapter 8), but cannot trigger 
representations of emotions as entities independent of the person, because the base noun 
is (nearly) always treated syntactically as a part of the person. This could explain why 
yolh-no 'pep, feelings', which seems related etymologically to abdominal body-parts, 
denotes an emotional part of the person and remains an animate-part noun. Whether 
incorporated or used externally, yolh-no raises its possessor like other animate-part 
nouns. 
"'421 '"'-' 
[PDF PAGE 447]
The language of emotions in Dalabon 
Indeed, in English or French, where body-part words can gain an emotional sense and the 
emotions are represented as independent entities, body-part possessor raising is not as 
systematic as in Dalabon. In these languages, raised-possessor constructions are also a 
common option (Tve got a belly-ache\ 'j'ai la jambe cassee' ('I've got a broken leg1)), yet 
there exist common alternatives where the body-part is easily and naturally treated as an 
autonomous argument ('my head is very sore', 'sajambe luifait ma/' ('his leg hurts him')). 
2.3.2 Body-part noun incorporation 
Another possible influence of the morphosyntactic properties of Dalabon body-part nouns 
(i.e. animate-part nouns) on emotion metaphors concerns the principles of noun 
incorporation. While possessor raising is quasi-obligatory with body-parts in descriptions 
of bodily matters, incorporation is clearly not obligatory in these contexts, but it is a 
preferred option. Examples (16) and (17) illustrate each construction (in both cases, the 
possessor is raised, as attested by the first person prefix nga- cross-referencing the 
possessor on the verb). The external construction in (17) is far less frequent than the noun 
incorporation construction in (16): less than ten occurrences in the corpora, 11 against 
more than a hundred incorporation constructions.

It is widely attested cross-linguistically that noun incorporation applies to absolutive 
arguments (S or 0): A arguments do not incorporate (see for instance Baker 1988:81). 
Since in Dalabon body-parts display a clear preference for incorporation in the semantic 
contexts at stake, we can expect a tendency to treat them as absolutive arguments, and to 
avoid expressing them as A. Therefore , they cannot occur in agentive semantic roles which

would represent them as forces or opponents (acting upon a patient). These tendencies
