2.3.3 Cross-linguistic comparison 
I have articulated two possible correlations between the morphosyntactic behavior of 
Dalabon body-part nouns (animate-part subclass) and the fact that Dalabon emotion 
metaphors represent emotions as parts or states of the person, not as independent 
entities, and even less as agents. First, the fact that body-parts (nearly always) raise their 
possessors to the function of argument means that they cannot be treated as arguments 
themselves. This could help explain why, even when body-part nouns gain an emotional 
sense, they are never treated as independent entities. Second, Dalabon also displays a 
strong preference for the incorporation of body-parts, which entails that body-parts 
preferably relate to the absolutive argument-and thus cannot be ergative. This could help 
explain why they are never treated as agents acting upon patient/passive experiencer. 
These hypotheses are intended as suggestions, not as demonstrations. They can only be 
refined, and eventually tested, by means of cross-linguistic comparison. Studying emotion 
metaphors in languages that make some use of body-part noun incorporation and/or 
possessor raising but also display some linguistic representation of emotions as 
independent entities and as agents would shed further light on the issue. Within Australia, 
Murrinh Patha (Walsh 1987), Mawng (Singer 2006) and other Iwaidjan languages (Evans 
2004) are good candidates for such studies; Enindhilyakwa is interesting as well to the 
extent that its body-part nouns incorporate, like in Dalabon, but do not raise their 
possessor in such a systematic fashion (Van Egmond 2012; Waddy n.d.). Outside of 
Australia, there are also many candidates for comparison (for instance Oneida (Iroquoian) 
(Michelson 2002:202), Zulu (Taylor & Mbense 1998:210), Gbaya (Africa, Ubangian, 
Roulon-Doko (in prep.), Papuan languages such as Koromu (Priestley 2002), to quote only 
a few where the metaphors of emotions have already been documented). 
Naturally, even if the above hypotheses were correct, one wouldn't expect straightforward 
matches. It seems naive to imagine that all languages which have, say, prominent body­
part incorporation, automatically rule out agentive emotion metaphors (i.e. forces or 
opponents emotions metaphors). However, by considering the phenomena at stake in

several languages, one may be able to identify recurring patterns of correlations between 
emotion metaphors, incorporability, possessor ra1s1ng, and possibly other 
morphosyntactic properties of emotion-related nouns. 
2.4 The preference for experiencer subjects 
Section 2.1 suggested a correlation between the nominal subclass membership of nouns 
for emotions or affects. Section 2.2 and 2.3 spelt out plausible (albeit hypothetical) 
correlations between the morphosyntactic behavior of Dalabon body-part nouns 
(animate-part nouns) and the fact that emotion nouns which derive from these nouns are 
never treated as independent arguments, even less agentive arguments. In the present 
section, I question the fact thatyirru 'conflict, anger' metaphors only marginally represent 
anger as an entity independent of the person, although yirru is a generic noun and not an 
animate-part noun. I suggest grammatical factors which could help explain this. 
As recalled above and discussed in Chapter 9 (1.3.2), yirru 'conflict, anger', a generic noun 
with no body-related denotation, is represented metaphorically as an entity independent 
of the person in one compound,yirru-ngalka 'conflict, anger'+ 'find', 'be(come) angry'. This 
correlates with the fact that in this compound, yirru is treated like other generic nouns, i.e. 
when incorporated it expresses the entire absolutive argument (8, repeated below). Thus, 
YIRRU 'conflict, anger' is treated as an autonomous argument, not as a part of a 
possessor-as a generic noun, yirru is not obligatorily possessed ( and as a matter of fact it 
. is never possessed).

Intransitive anger compounds like yirru-burlh(mu) 'conflict, anger'+'come out', 'be(come) 
angry' entail a conflict between the rules of noun incorporation associated with the 
generic incorporated noun yirru 'conflict, anger', and argument mapping expectations 
assigned to intransitive emotional predicates. According to the rules of generic noun 
incorporation, the generic noun should be cross-referenced as an argument on the verb­
and so the person prefix should always be the third person singular prefix ka- . Such 
constructions, where the invariable A argument is an affect, are reported in Murrinh Patha 
(Walsh 1987), Mawng (Singer 2006:216-220) and other Iwaidjan languages (Evans 2004) 
for various emotions, among them anger. However, in Dalabon, in compliance with the 
preferred argument mapping for intransitive emotion predicates, with all intransitive 
anger predicates, it is the experiencer that gets cross-referenced on the verb. As we see in 
(19), yirru-burlh(mu) 'conflict, anger' +'come out', 'be( come) angry1 the person prefix is the 
first person singular nga-, cross-referencing the experiencer. Thus, with intransitive 
YIRRU predicates, argument mapping regularity overrides subclass-specific syntactic rules 
of noun incorporation, and the compounds lexicalize a subcategorization pattern which 
does not match the nominal subclass requirements of the incorporated noun . Strictly 
speaking, such compounds are no longer interpretable as noun incorporation 
constructions, unless we reassign yirru 'conflict, anger' to the animate-part nominal 
subclass. 
As a result of this shift in subcategorization, these YIRRU compounds, although they are 
based on a generic noun and not a body-part noun, do not yield independent entity 
,..., 425,..., 
[PDF PAGE 451]
The language of emotions in Dalabon 
metaphors of anger. If anything, these compounds look as if the genenc noun yzrru 
'conflict, anger' is being treated syntactically as an animate-part noun. If such a reanalysis 
applied, compounds like yirru-burlh{mu) 'conflict, anger'+'come out', 'be(come) angry' 
would instantiate the metaphor EMOTIONS ARE PARTS OF THE PERSON. This results from the 
fact that the regularity of argument mapping in intransitive emotional predicates, where 
experiencer subjects are preferred (more than three-quarter of the predicates, see Chapter 
5, 2.2) overrides syntactic constraints imposed by nominal subclass membership of the 
noun which serves as a base to the metaphor. This preference for experiencer subjects 
correlates with the preference for possessor raising in physical affects and bodily 
processes intransitive predicates, where the animate experiencer must be raised to the 
status of subject, matching the standard subcategorization pattern for intransitive verbs of 
affect. The preference for marking experiencer as subject and for raising the possessor are 
obviously two sides of the same coin. 
Note that this alone does not preclude the representation of the emotion as an 
independent argument. At this stage, I have no hypothesis as to why yirru 'conflict, anger' 
is not represented as an ergative argument in transitive predicates of the type 'anger got 
down on me' for instance. Such representations are found in Dalabon with bar-no 'pain'. 
With anger, however, the language has selected metaphors which do not channel this type 
of representation. 
Again, the hypotheses above are not demonstrations but suggestions. They require further 
· exploration by means of cross-linguistic comparison and testing, where patterns of 
correlations between types of metaphors and some argument subcategorization 
preferences could be identified. 
3. Conclusion 
The present chapter points towards hypothetical linguistic explanations as to why 
Dalabon emotion metaphors mostly represent emotions as states or parts of the person, 
and not as entities independent of the person. This may be constrained by various 
grammatical features, such as the nominal subclass system and the morphosyntactic 
properties of these subclasses, including preferences for possessor raising and noun 
incorporation. Another syntactic preference of Dalabon, namely the preference for 
~426 ~ 
[PDF PAGE 452]
Chapter 11 + Excursus: The influence of grammar? 
experiencer subjects with emotion predicates, could also play a role. These plausible 
factors leave a lot of facts unexplained, and their mention here is suggestive. The point in 
this chapter was not to reach conclusions, but to indicate directions for future research. 
Ultimately, the question of the correlation between grammatical features and emotion 
metaphors, like all issues venturing into the problem of linguistic relativity, can only be 
tackled by means of cross-linguistic comparison, as mentioned throughout the above 
sections. 
Another relevant consideration is that only linguistic factors were considered here, but 
other factors may also come into play. It was argued in Chapter 8 (Section 4) that Dalabon 
metaphorical representations of emotions as states of the person correlate with the way 
Dalabon speakers and their descendants deal with emotions, and in particular with 
emotion management strategies (see Chapter 2, 4.3). Therefore, one may hypothesize that 
shared representations and cultural habits also contribute to shaping emotion metaphors. 
If this influence operates, then speakers of radically different languages, living in culturally 
comparable environments, should share similar metaphors. In the context at stake here, 
studying emotion metaphors in Barunga Kriol could shed some light on this question. 
Alternatively, could metaphors influence emotion management practices? If so, one should 
expect the borrowing of metaphors (from English into Kriol for instance) to entail 
behavioral changes, identifiable for instance in emotion mai:_iagement behaviors. As 
pointed out in the first section of this chapter, the interplay between the grammatical 
architecture of a language, its linguistic representation of emotions, and the 
conceptualization, experience of and attitude of speakers towards emotions deserves 
further exploration. Cross-linguistic studies of emotion language across several Australian 
languages, and further, should shed some light on this question.

12 Conclusion 
In this work, I have set out to describe emotional linguistic features, both expressive and 
descriptive, in Dalabon, a severely endangered south-western Arnhem Land language of 
the Gunwinyguan family (non-Pama-Nyungan). Like most languages in the world, and like 
many Australian languages in particular, Dalabon uses body-part words in lexical 
descriptions of emotions. One of the questions to be answered was that of the role of body­
parts in the emotion lexicon, a question that has not received a detailed answer in 
previous works. 
The documentation of the emotion language in Dalabon revealed a wealth of both 
expressive and descriptive features. After setting my theoretical framework and the 
ethnographic and linguistic contexts in chapters 1 to 3, I described expressive features in 
Chapter 4. The rest of the work, i.e. the other seven chapters (5 to 11), is dedicated to the 
description of the lexicon and the discussion of the role of body-parts. Some body-parts 
yield emotion metaphors. After discussing the linguistic and cognitive status of metaphors 
in Chapter 7, I described Dalabon body-based metaphors in Chapter 8. Chapter 9 
presented Dalabon metaphors where the body plays a lesser role. Moving away from 
metaphors, Chapter 10 showed that the contribution of body-parts to the emotion lexicon 
is not only metaphorical. Body-parts are also used to articulate precise descriptions of 
emotional behaviors, and through this function they also gain further semantic 
connotations. Based on these uses of body-parts, new linguistic forms are produced, which 
may in turn suggest new conceptual metaphors to speakers. In Chapter 11, I elaborated on 
the question of the influence of language on metaphorical representations, suggesting 
directions for future research around this question. In what follows, I briefly recapitulate 
the main points established throughout the work, following the order of the chapters. 
""' 4 2 8 ""' 
[PDF PAGE 454]
Conclusion 
1. Expressive features 
The main Dalabon expressive features presented in this work, in Chapter 4, are 
diminutives, interjections, and prosodic features. While descriptive features (the lexicon) 
are also significant, expressive features are more prominent by far in spontaneous speech. 
In addition, they express culturally central categories such as compassion for instance, 
towards which they converge, and which is not particularly well represented by 
descriptive, lexical resources. Thus, expressive features play a very central role. 
2. The lexicon 
Nevertheless, emotional descriptive resources, mainly lexical, are also available to 
Dalabon speakers. Dalabon displays a fairly large emotion lexicon (c. 160 lexemes), which 
is presented in chapters 5 and 6. Most lexemes are predicates (there is only a handful of 
nouns), and many lexemes are compound predicates of the form [noun+predicate]. The 
noun is very often a body-part or an attribute of the person, i.e. nouns of the animate-part 
morphosyntactic subclass. These morphological structures resemble noun incorporation 
constructions. Indeed, some of the compounds are probably lexicalized noun 
incorporation constructions; others are not, but speakers nevertheless tend to assign 
literal interpretations to them following the rules of syntactic noun incorporation. These 
literal interpretations yield metaphors. 
Apart from a very few exceptions and subtleties, the syntax of Dalabon emotion p~edicates 
is relatively regular. The predicates divide into three classes presenting distinctive 
argument subcategorization patterns. The largest class, comprising more than three­
quarters of the predicates, includes intransitive predicates, where the experiencer is 
always encoded as the only argument, S. Another, smaller class is transitive, and maintains 
the experiencer as its first argument A, treating the stimulus 0. There are also some 
causative predicates, where the experiencer is encoded as 0, and the stimulus as A. 
Chapter 6 dealt with the semantics of the lexicon and provided some ethnographic details 
about the contexts in which various emotion words are used. Previous anthropological 
works on emotions (in particular Myers 1986) demonstrated the primacy of interpersonal 
emotions associated with 'relatedness'-compassion, anger, shame-among some 
,..., 429,..., 
[PDF PAGE 455]
The language of emotions in Dalabon 
Australian groups (e.g. the Pintupi for Myers). Not only do such emotions feed emotional 
experience, but they also shape moral values, and with them, social structures and 
behaviors. Conforming to this tendency, many Dalabon emotion words denote other­
oriented emotions: anger and other conflict-related emotions, compassion, grief, shame. In 
fact, many words are polysemous between self- and other-oriented emotions. As with the 
Pintupi described by Myers, these emotions play a strong structuring role among the 
Dalabon. However, many Dalabon emotion words denote emotions that have nothing to do 
with moral norms imposed by the values of 'relatedness', but describe feelings proper to 
the person, associated with the will, one's desires, enthusiasm and energy. These 
emotions, and the autonomy of individuals with respect to emotions, are often discussed, 
and rarely dismissed. Thus, relatedness is not the only emotional value in the Dalabon 
social and conceptual landscape. 
Another remark relevant to lexical categories is that there is no straightforward 
correlation between the existence of a lexeme for a given emotion, and the cultural 
salience of this emotion. For instance, compassion is culturally central, and emotions 
related to mourning are conceptually salient, but these emotions are not well represented 
lexically. On the other hand, there are some words for talking about love and sexual desire, 
but these emotions seem relatively backgrounded, at least for the speakers I worked with. 
3. Metonymy and metaphor 
As mentioned above, many Dalabon emotional lexemes are compounds, and many of these 
compounds include a body-part. Some of the body-parts recur across large sets of 
compounds, with a range of predicates. Several of these sets yield metaphors inspired by 
somatic metonymies. The main body-part yielding metaphors is kangu-no 'belly', which 
participates in tropes related to resistance, destruction and fluidity of the belly. These 
metaphors are engraved in the Dalabon lexicon, and therefore highly conventionalized. 
However, they are not opaque to speakers, who perceive them and tend to elaborate 
semiotically upon some of them. There are also some relatively marginal metaphors 
involving the heart. Although not a body-part, but morphosyntactically associated with 
parts of the person, the noun yolh-no 'pep, feelings' also participates in metaphors, in 
particular mobility metaphors. A particularity of these body-based emotion metaphors is 
that they always represent emotions as states of the person, or as parts of the person: 
"' 43 0 "' 
[PDF PAGE 456]
Conclusion 
emotions are represented metaphorically as states of the belly, or as a state of the yolh-no 
'pep, feelings', which is in turn represented linguistically as an inalienable part of the 
person. 
This particularity also applies-albeit less systematically-to non-body-based metaphors. 
Metaphors for anger in particular, instantiated by compounds formed with the noun yirru 
'conflict, anger', also mostly represent emotions as states of the person. With these 
compounds, however, there are exceptions, and anger is sometimes represented 
metaphorically as an entity independent of the person. Dalabon metaphors for anger also 
differ from body-based Dalabon metaphors, and from other anger metaphors across the 
world, in that they are not inspired by somatic responses to anger. Instead, anger is 
presented as a self-developing living entity, often compared to poison, disease, or affects 
such as pain (which are not somatic reactions to anger). These metaphors are probably 
inspired by behaviors associated with anger, and by the negative moral status of anger. 
Dalabon makes no significant use of the cross-linguistically widespread metaphor 
involving representations of anger as heat and pressure in a container. Altogether, 
Dalabon anger metaphors are interesting because they diverge both from other Dalabon 
emotion metaphors and from anger metaphors in other languages. This raises questions as 
to why anger attracts this particular treatment. 
4. Body-parts and emotional behaviors 
Not all [body-part+predicate] emotional compounds are metaphorical. In a large number 
of emotional compounds, and more specifically with predicates denoting emotional 
behaviors, body-parts specify which part of the experiencer is involved in the emotional 
behavior in question. These compounds thus allow speakers to say that one is 'angry from 
the hands' when gesticulating, or 'shying away from the mouth' when one is too shy to 
talk. In such compounds, the contribution of body-parts is not primarily metaphorical, but 
(semi -)compositional. This principle of composition yields half a dozen semi-productive 
sets of compounds denoting emotional behaviors, each based on one type of emotional 
behavior (anger, avoidance due to shame, sulking, laughing ... ). Each of these sets differs 
slightly from the others, yet altogether they display family resemblances, and as a result 
formal analogy operates between the sets to produce further compounds and assign 
meaning to them. Some body-parts recur throughout several sets, with semi-regular 
""' 4 31 ""' 
[PDF PAGE 457]
The language of emotions in Dalabon 
semantic contributions. As a result, several visible body-parts and a couple of predicates 
gain regular emotional connotations. Invisible body-parts, such as KANGU 'belly' in 
particular, systematically contribute the semantic feature 'emotionally1 throughout a 
number of compounds, matching its metaphorical representation. 
5. Conceptual motivations and formal motivations 
While metaphors and metonymies play an important part in the emotion lexicon, they are 
not the only principles driving lexical formation and semantic extension . Rather, the 
emotional behavior sets involving body-parts seem to expand following principles of 
compositionality and formal analogy. Thus, formal-as opposed to conceptual-principles 
also yield semantic extension. In addition, some compounds formed on the basis of 
analogy may in turn suggest emotion metaphors, so that the canonical direction of 
influence between conceptual and linguistic metaphors is inverted. In the canonical 
cognitivists
1 
view on metaphor, any linguistic metaphor results from a conceptual 
metaphor. In the Dalabon emotion lexicon, we find cases where the reverse may be 
possible. The idea of the influence of formal linguistic principles upon the metaphorical 
representation of emotions is further explored in Chapter 11. This short, speculative 
chapter points towards directions for future cross-linguistic research, by identifying 
hypothetical plausible influences of Dalabon grammatical features upon Dalabon emotion 
metaphors.

djare adj. 
Djare means like, love or want. It can 
denote taste , for instance for types of 
food (1 ), or affection , either for relatives 
(2), or sexually oriented affection (3). 
When talking about love for a person , 
benefactive constructions are used. 
Benefactive constructions are also 
sometimes used with inanimates , when 
the sense is 'like' rather than want ( 4). 
Conversely , djare can be used without a 
benefactive even though it applies to an 
animate , when the sense is 'want' (5). 
Djare is also often found followed by a 
complement clause (6, 7), where the 
sense is usually ambiguous between 
'like ' ('feel like') and 'want' . 
.,... (1) [Kofi] mak nga-djare. I don 't 
like coffee.

marnu-yininj djah-marnu-djare. Me 
and my little sister have come back , she 
says to their grandmother. I love you she 
tells her. 
.,... (3) Djah-kakku-marnu-djare. He 
[your husband] really loves you.

kangu-mon adj. Lit: 'belly +good ' .

kangu-yowyow(mu) v.i. Lit: 'belly+flow'. 
Feel good , experience positive feelings. 
Kangu-yowyow(mu) is used when 
someone is pleased because of some 
positive , but relatively minor, daily 
event (1, 2). Benefactive constructions 
can mean either 'be pleased about 
someone' (self-oriented, 3) or 'be well­
disposed towards someone ' (i.e. 
emotions targeting others, 4). Kangu­
yowyow(mu) can also refer to a more 
durable state, talking about people of 
good temperament , who are usually 
happy (5), In this dispositional sense, 
kangu-yowyow(mu) can also refer to 
good feelings for others, and thus mean 
kind, generous (6).

yolh-burrama adj. Lit: 
'pep /feelings+good '. 
Feel good. The sense is more often 
emotional. Yolh-burrama was sometimes 
used to describe 'being in a good mood ', 
i.e. feeling good in this particular 
moment (self-oriented , 1). At other times 
it meant 'be a good person ', referring to 
someone 's positive feelings for others 
(2). In some cases, yolh-burrama refer to 
a more general state, including physical 
well-being (3). Yolh-burrama is far less 
frequent than yolh-mon , and also less 
frequent than kangu-burrama . Kriol: 
gudbinji. 
...,. (1) Mak ka-kakku-yolh-burrama. 
Kah-dje-kolmu, bah buyirrhwalungh 
mak ka-kakku-dje-kolmu kahke, kah­
kangu-murduk. She's not really feeling 
good. She looks cheerful, but deep inside 
she's not really cheerful. 
...,. (2) Kah-marnu­
kangu-yowyowminj, bah mak ka-
kakku-yolh-burrama. Kah-yolh-weh­
yolh-weh nunh bah njel kah­
drekimhminj. He was kind to us, but he 
didn't really mean well. He's nasty, he 
ripped us off. 
...,. (3) Dabarngh mak nga-yolh­
burrama-mini. Dubmi ngah-yolh­
burrama. Yesterday I was feeling well 
[I was feeling crooked]. Today I feel 
good. 
Syn: yolh-mon ; kangu-burrama . Ant: 
yolh-weh .

yolh-mon(-mun) adj. Lit: 
'pep/feelings+good( +INCH)'. 
1) Feel good, either emotionally or 
physically. Yolh-mon is the most 
common emotional term in Dalabon. 
When the sense is emotional, it can be 
self-oriented (be happy, be pleased: 1 to 
4). Alternatively, the feelings can target 
someone, in which case the sense is 'get 
on (with someone)' (5 and 6), or 'be 
kind' ( a disposition, 7). This sense often 
occurs with benefactive constructions 
(6). Yolh-mon can also mean 'feel good 
physically' (8). Sometimes the sense is 
both emotional and physical at a time 
(9). 
~ (1) Kakkak-no kardu kah-lng-yolh­
mon. Bulu kah-marnu-njerrh-ye­
dudjminj ma. His grandmother will 
surely be happy. He's bringing the dead 
[kangaroo] back to them alright. 
~ (2) Dah-milh-djonghmu, dohkardu 
dah-ngalbak-djonghmu. Kuku-yolh­
mon-mun. You kiss [the little girl] on 
her forehead, or on her cheek. To make 
her feel good. 
~ (3) Ngah-marnu-yolh-mon-minj, 
mulah-ngan-kun. I'm feeling better 
about my aunt [ who passed away]. 
~ (4) Rolu kahnun, kah­
warhwarhmu, kah-yolh-mon, 
kuluhkuluh-no-kah. That dog is 
wagging its tail, it's happy to be with its 
master. 
~ (5) Yo, djah-lng-marnu-yenjdjung 
kanh, kah-mon, kah-lng-yolh-mon, 
njing-kun. Yeah, he speaks to you now, 
it's OK, he feels good about you (he gets 
along with you). 
~ (6) Mak bulu nga-marnu­
yenjdjung, mak bulu nga-marnu-yolh­
mon. Wadda-ngan-kih-kah ngey-karn 
ngah-ni. I don't speak to them, I don't 
get along with them. I stay by myself at 
my own place. 
~ (7) Yibung nunh kanh kah-yolh­
mon, bulu kah-naHnan. She's kind this 
one, she looks after them. 
~ (8) Djah-njenguyungiyan, djah-lng­
dokkiyan ... Djah-wonarruniyan, djah­
lng-yolh-mon-muniyan! You'll sleep , 
you'll wake up ... See how you feel, 
you'll feel good! 
~ (9) Kah-yolh-mon-minj. Kanh kah­
kolh-nomung, bukah-yolh-mon-wong. 
He's feeling better now. This [petrol] he 
sniffed, it made him feel good. 
Syn: kangu-burrama (partial); kangu­
mon (partial). Ant: yolh-weh; kangu­
weh-no; kangu-weh-mun. 
2) Feel like doing something, when yolh­
mon is followed by a sentence describing 
a possible future event. 
~ Yolh-no mak ka-yolh-mon kah­
boniyan. Kah-warndih. As for him, he 
won't go, he doesn't feel like it. He's not 
up to it. 
~ Djah-yolh-mon-miniyan, kardu ... 
djeh-burruniyan. Do you want us two 
to ... fight together? 
yolh-murduk adj. Lit: 
'pep/feelings+hard/strong'. Yolh-murduk 
is a less common alternative for kangu­
murduk. It has the same senses. 
Syn: kal!gu-murduk. 
1) Be socially confident: typically self­
assertive, in particular in conflicts. 
~ Kardu yirru bale-durrun, duway­

2) Have negative feelings, not be open to 
others, i.e. be austere (self-oriented) or

ka-yolh-ni, kah-dja-ni yibung-karn

yolh-ngun v.t. Lit: 'pep /feelings+eat ' . 
Yolh-ngu,n is used to ask pseudo­

or when they don 't understand what they 
. do or feel. ;Literally, these questions

with you? ' . Often there is a negative 
connotation , but sometimes the speaker 
simply expresses an interrogation. Yolh­
ngu,n is not used in other contexts.

yolh-weh adj. Lit: 'pep/feelings +bad ' . 
,.., 464 ,.., 
[PDF PAGE 490]
Feel bad. Yolh-weh is a generic term 
which can apply to all sorts of negative 
states. Yolh-weh is more commonly used 
to talk about negative feelings (1-'7), but 
it can also mean feel physically bad (8). 
When the sense is emotional , it can 
describe self-oriented feelings like 
feeling upset, sad, unhappy (1 to 3). 
Alternatively , and more rarely, y olh-weh 
can refer to feelings that target other 
people (be angry, be in a bad mood , 4 
and 5). This sense can refer to a 
momentary state, or to someone's 
disposition to be in a bad mood 
(personality feature: be selfish, mean, 
nasty, 6 and 7).

Appendix 2: Body-Part Lexicon 
This short lexicon lists only the body-parts used in emotional compounds. It includes 
examples from various corpora, including many published in Evans, Merlan & 
Tukumba's first Dalabon Dictionary (2004). 
B - b 
berru-no n.PAW 
1) Chest, either on humans or animals , 
typically the flat area above the breast, 
between the shoulders. 
~ Rolu kah-berru-djabdi. The dog's 
sitting up with his chest sticking out (i.e. 
on his hind legs). 
~ Yibung-karn nahda kah-berru­
borled en nunda mahkih nahda kah­
berru-borled. And him there, he' s 
turning his chest (i.e. turning his back on 
someone) , and this one as well there 
she's turning her chest (turning her back 
on someone). 
~ Nab-no mah nidjarrah bibbi berru­
no-kah bulah-dadjdadjka. And the 
mother [ of a young boy being initiated] , 
they cut her breast here, on the chest. 
2) With locative suffix, and appropriate 
pronominal suffix: in front of. 
~ Nguy berru-ngan-kah kah-rung. 
D - d 
dalu-no 
1) n.PAW Mouth. Like 'mouth' in 
English, dalu-no means both the outside 
and the inside part of the mouth. It refers 
to both humans and animals' mouths. 
The beak of a bird, however, is called 
dje-no 'nose'. 
~ Kah-dalu-moh-ni-moh-ni. 
[Someone with rash on their lips.] He's 
"' 4 73 "' 
The fire is burning in front of me. 
3) n.PIW The front (of an object). 
~ Berru-no-kah kah-ngey-di bulah­
bim-buninj berru-no-kah. There is a 
name written on the front [ of his T­
shirt]. 
4) n.? Tobacco: block tobacco with a 
mark in the middle. Said to be 'flat like 
(a) chest' . 
~ Beka berru-no nikiniki ngey-no. 
The block tobacco , it's called nikiniki. 
5) directional . With a word indicating a 
direction ( cardinal , up, down): 
directional. 
~ Njing-karn mah djah-ninginj 
berru-walum, djah-durduHminj. As 
for you, you were sitting with your chest 
to the south, you sat on your own side. 
~ Kah-hon nahda berru-·yirrh. It goes 
upwards there. 
got rash on the mouth. 
~ Modjarrki kah-dalu-barrminj, 
kah-dalu-dabkarrinj. The crocodile 
opened and shut its mouth. 
~ Nunh biyi kaye-ngungun mey, 
dalu-no-walung kah-burlhka nguh-no­
kah. When someone eats food, it goes 
down from the mouth to the stomach. 
~ Kikkik dabo-no, bulnu yilah-
[PDF PAGE 499]
marnu-yung dalu-bulng-kah, kah­
yenjHyenjdjung kanunh manjh, dalu­
bulng-kah, nunh kanunh wurdurd 
balah-Ing-yenjdjung. [When children 
don't speak early enough ,] the egg of the 
kikkik bird, we put it in their mouth , the 
bird sings in their mouth , and then the 
child will talk. 
2) n.PJW. Opening (e.g. of bottle). 
...,_ Bodul-kun dalu-no bulah-dalu­
dabka. The bottle 's opening has been 
sealed (with a cork). 
dje-no n.PAW 
1) Nose (including nose-bridge) on 
humans , snout on animals. This is the 
most salient sense for most species. 
...,_ Ngah-dje-njirdmey. I sweated from 
my nose. 
...,_ Kah-dje-werlhwerl. (The possum) is 
hanging nose-down from the tree. 
_ ...,_ Yalah-mukkarrinj radjdja-kah, 
dje-no yalah-dje-darrkminj. We buried 
ourselves in the sand, with our noses 
sticking out. 
2) Nostril , on humans and animals (this 
is the most salient sense on crocodiles). 
...,_ Dje-yabbunh nidjarraberdah, kah­
dje-dun-ni nuhkahbe. Here are the two 
nostrils , the nose-holes there . 
3) Beak. 
...,_ Nunda ngurrurdu. Mumu-no, dje­
no. This is an emu. Its eyes, its beak. 
4) Face (a secondary sense). 
...,_ Malambibbi kah-dje-moymirrinj. 
Malambibbi (bat) has a squashed up 
face. 
...,_ Kah-dje-bimburrinj bim-yih. She 
painted her face with kaolin. 
...,_ Wurdi ngah-dje-werleberrkmi. Oh 
dear, I'm all wrinkled [my face hangs 
down] . 
n.PJW. 
5) Branch stubs on tree, or a small 
nostril-like hole in a tree through which 
bees go in and out to their nest. 
...,_ Yurduh ngalk-no, yalk ngalkngalk­
no, rorlbban ngalk-no, nunh diwarrah 
dje-no, modjarnh-dje-no, belinjdjan­
burlubburlu-dje-no, bod-no kanh 
kaye-njimu. We say the 'mouth ' for 
yurduk, yalk, and lorlbban sugarbags , 
but the 'nose' for diwarrah , modjarnh 
and belinjdjan-burlubburlu sugarbags , 
for where the bee enters. 
6) Hook of spear-thrower or woomera, 
to which spear is attached. 
...,_ Borndok kah-yidjnjan. Nunda 
borndok dje-no. He's holding a 
woomera (spear-thrower). And this is the 
hook of the woomera. 
djud-no n.PAW Back of neck, nape of neck, 
for humans or animals . 
...,_ Djud-ngan ngah-djud-kardminj. 
My neck is stiff, I have a sore neck. 
Djud-no-kah bulah-dadjka, kodj-no 
bulah-kan bulah-ngun. They cut [the 
crocodile] at the level of the neck, they 
take the head and eat it. 
dolku-no n.PAW Back , either on humans or 
on animals. Animals like snakes or 
mollusks are also described as having a 
back. Dolku-no is not clearly attested as 
a label for the spine (which is dolku-mo­
no ), although some occurrences may be 
slightly ambiguous. Kriol: bekbon . 
...,_ Kah-dolku-derrengdi dulh-kah. He 
is leaning his back against the tree. 
...,_ Kah-kirdmun dolku-no, bard­
karlang-no kah-Ing-kirdmun, rakmo­
no ... Mak kanh ka-Ing-bobon kah-ni. 
His back is crippled , his knees are 
crippled , his hip ... He can 't walk , he 
stays in one place. 
K-k 
kangu-no n.PAW 
1) Belly. External body-part : front part 
of humans or standing animals 
kangaroos , often rounded . Lower parts 
of crocodiles , fish, emus . Kriol: binji. 
""' 4 7 4 ""' 
...,_ Kangu-barmiyi djokbinj. It's 
yellow-bellied , that djokbinj. 
2) Belly. Receptacle: container of 
abdominal organs , usually lower 
abdomen but sometimes considered to 
[PDF PAGE 500]
encompass the whole torse. This is 
where a woman carries a child. Kangu­
no is represented linguistically as the 
container of some mental representations 
and internal conflicts, and as the locus of 
emotions. 
...,. Kah-yaw-marrun, yirrh-walung 
kangu-no-kah. She's carrying a child, 
inside in her belly. 
...,. Kah-kodj-wokarrun kanihdja, 
nunh yirru, boyenj kah-yidjnjan. 
Kangu-no-kah. He's wondering, he has 
a big conflict there. In his belly. 
...,. Mak buka-bawoyan, kah-dja­
marnu-djare, kangu-no-kah kah­
dorrung-ni. She won't leave him, she 
really loves him, he's there in her heart 
[belly]. 
n.PIW. 
3) The inside, the core center of 
something. Yalang kanh dulh bukah­
kangu-lorrk-won, [ ... ] ka-h-dulh­
ngungun, kah-Ing-kangu-lorrk-mun 
kanh kah-rakkan. The termites empty 
the core of the tree, they eat up the tree, 
then its core is empty and it falls. 
kodj-no n.PA w. 
1) Crown of head or head, on humans 
and animals. The crown of the head is 
the primary denotation (1 ), i.e. the one 
speakers give first. A lot of the time, the 
context does not allow us to differentiate 
between reference to the crown of the 
head and to the whole head (2). There 
are cases where the referent is clearly the 
whole head (3, 4). Kodj-no is sometimes 
represented linguistically as the locus of 
thought and intellectual functions (5). 
...,. (1) Duway-no bukah-Ing-marnu­
yin, nunda ngey ngah-dulubuninj, 
dah-lng-kodj-ngun. Her husband says 
to her, I speared a kangaroo, you can eat 
the head [ after the skull has been split to 
separate the crown]. 
...,. (2) Djorrkkun kah-kodj-dodorrun, 
kah-budjbun kurlba-no djehneng 
wanjh kah-kodj-dorrun. (It's like) rock 
possums strike their heads, when they 
piss it's like they've cut their heads in 
mourning (leaving a red streak on the 
rock). 
...,. (3) Bidjdjirri yilah-kodj-bang, 
ngurrah-kodj-bang. We bite the head 
off file snakes. 
...,. ( 4) Kah-kodj-dih nunda. Dorrung­
no kah-kodj-dih. This one has no head . 
The body has no head. 
...,. (5) Wanjh bulah-lng-nang bulah­
Ing-me, kardu ka-yin kodj-no-kah . 
Now they saw me and caught me, she 
must be thinking in her head. 
n.PIW. 
2) Edible part of a root or vegetable . 
...,. Didjkala kanh yale-yin kodj-no 
yaw-no kah-yidjnjan bah mey 
didjkala yilah-ngun. What we call 
didjkala, it has a small bulb, but we 
consume this edible part. 
koh-no n.PAW 
Not very commonly used as a noun, but 
frequent in compounds. Sometimes the 
word has a more concrete meaning , 
'eyes'. Sometimes it is more abstract: 
'sight', 'gaze', 'look'. 
...,. Koh-no kahnunda mumu-no 
kuhyin. [Pointing to the eyes on a 
drawing,] koh-no is this one, the eyes 
indeed. 
...,. [Koh-no], mumu-no-yih kanh kah­
kurnh-Qan. Koh-no , she looks around 
with her eyes. 
Syn: mumu-no (partial). 
kom-no n.PA w. 
Neck, back of neck, for humans or 
animals. 
...,. Kom-ngu djah-kom-yidjnjarrun 
burrkunh-walungh. You're holding 
(the back of) your neck from both sides 
(i.e. with both hands). 
...,. Ngurl-wirb! Bukah-ngurl-wirbme 
bukah-dja-lng-kom-dengkoHminj. 
Rip! He ripped his heart out and 
knocked him in the back of the neck. 
...,. Ngah-kom-bahrdirrinj djarridj-yih 
yulu-yih ngah-Ing-kom-ngurlmu. I 
painted my neck with charcoal, with 
earth, I have a black neck.

langu-no n.PAW 
I) Hand of humans , front paws of 
. animals , also back paws for reptiles. 
Kriol: bingga, fingga. 
...,. Mak wuku-langu-rokan. [Ifmy

...,. Yirrkbadj kah-yawayawan djenj,

Syn: ngarrinj-no. 
2) Digits of the above (hand , front paw, 
back paw when they are called langu­
no). Kriol: bingga, fingga.

medmo-no n.PA W 
...,. Wirrimah kardu worrbbamh-wurd

men-no n.PAW 
The set of one 's ideas , judgments , 
opinions ; it can also translate as mind, 
consciousness. Men-no can connote 
social mindedness , respect for others. By 
far the most common use of men-no is in 
constructions of the type 'kah-yin, men­
no', 'he thinks , in his mind ' . Animals 
can have men-no if they are deemed 
intelligent. Kriol : aidiya, maind.

mo-no 
1) n.P AW Bone, bones, either as a 
single bone or as remains. This applies 
to human bones as well as to animals, 
including fish bones. Compounds can 
refer to particular bones in the human

Appendix 4: Emotive interjections 
This appendix presents examples of interjections listed in Table 4, Chapter 4, but not 
discussed in the chapter. 
The emotive interjections ah and ahah are not illustrated here because they occurred in 
isolation, so that there was no linguistic context to the examples. They were used for 
instance when commenting on movies, when the speakers were emotionally involved and 
considered a striking or puzzling scene. All the other interjections listed in Table 4 of 
Chapter 4 are exemplified, following the order of the table.

Appendix 7: Speakers' biographies 
Maggie Tukumba [skin name: Ngarridjan] 
c.1940/45 
Maggie Tukumba, a member of the Wakmarranj Dalabon clan, was born on the Arnhem 
Land plateau and spent her early childhood there. Her family's main language was 
Dalabon. They stayed in the bush at least until World War II. They then shifted to 
Maranboy, between Katherine and the contemporary Barunga, where Maggie
1
s parents 
worked at the tin mine. She learnt English and Barunga Kriol there. Later, she settled in 
Barunga, where she briefly attended school, before being married and having children. 
Maggie and her family shifted back to the Bulman region, closer to Dalabon land, after the 
Northern Territory Land Rights Act 1976 was passed. When Weemol was created, 
following the outstation movement, Maggie settled there with her family and has been 
living there since. She likes Weemol, expresses strong attachment to the region, and avoids 
travelling, except to Katherine for compelling reasons. 
Maggie is a full speaker of Dalabon, which is her first language. Although Kriol is the 
language she uses more naturally for daily interactions, Maggie
1
s Dalabon is very fluent, 
thorough and rich. She is also a very talented and dedicated consultant. She is a purist and 
does not like mixing Dalabon with English or Kriol. She is nevertheless a strong advocate 
of Kriol. She knows Mayali and probably some Rembarrnga. Her mastery of English is 
limited and she is not literate. 
Lily Bennett [ skin name: Bangarn] 
1951 
Lily Bennett reports being born in the bush, and arriving at Barunga after being taken 
there by force, with her family, when she was about 8 y.o. (in the meantime, they were 
probably at the Maranboy mine, close to Barunga). Lily attended school in Barunga (where 
several languages were spoken and Dalabon was backgrounded), and later the Batchelor 
Institute of Indigenous Tertiary Education (in the town of Batchelor, closer to Darwin). She 
married and had children in Barunga, where she worked at the school and then at the 
health center. After the Northern Territory Land Rights Act 1976 was passed, she returned 
to the Bulman region, closer to her homeland, and lived in Weemol for a number of years. 
She came back to live closer to Katherine, in Beswick, around the year 2000. She lives 
there most of the time, with occasional visits to Weemol and other communities. 
Lily Bennett
1
s Dalabon is fluent and she may be considered a full-speaker, although she 
has less vocabulary than Maggie Tukumba, and is less at-ease with the grammar. Her 
English proficiency is high and she is fully literate. Lily's Dalabon is significantly influenced 
by Kriol and English. Her mother and father were both Dalabon. Lily learnt Dalabon first; 
then Mayali. Her father
1
s mother was Dalabon with Rembarrnga affiliations, and .LilY. learnt 
,.., 520,.., 
[PDF PAGE 546]
Rembarrnga with her. Lily learnt Kriol with the other children at school. Traditional 
languages were banned from the school (their use was punished). Back home, Lily reports 
addressing her parents in Kriol, while they replied either in Kriol or in Dalabon. Dalabon 
was spoken in Weemol until the end of the 1990s, and Lily reports that her mastery of 
traditional languages improved while she lived there. 
Queenie Brennan [skin name: Bangarn] 
Born c. 1950 
Queenie Brennan currently lives between Barunga, Katherine and Oenpelli. She has family 
in each of these three places. She spent some time in Pine Creek, north-west of Katherine, 
as a child, and attended school there for a while. 
Queenie explains that her mother taught her Mayali and her father taught her Dalabon. 
She learnt Barunga Kriol with her peers, like everyone of this generation in the region. Her 
English is excellent and she is fully literate. Mayali, Kriol, and to some extent English, are 
languages of daily interaction for her, while Dalabon is a more rarely used third language. 
However, Queenie has dedicated some time and effort to learning more Dalabon recently, 
and is now a fluent semi-speaker. She is attached to it as her father
1
s language, and aware 
of the threat bearing upon it. 
t Jimmy Wesan [skin name: Kodjok] 
Born c. 1935- 2011. 
Jimmy Wesan, a member of the Bulaldjdja Dalabon clan, was born on Dalabon land, in the 
Bulman region. He lived there with his family until mid-childhood, and during that time he 
was exposed to ancestral languages only. His family left the region around World War II. 
They settled in Dendengel (near contemporary Beswick). Jimmy went to school and learnt 
English and Barunga Kriol there. He spent the rest of his life in this region, where he 
worked, married and had children. He still lived in Beswick when he died in 2011. 
Dalabon was Jimmy Wesan's first language, and he was thus a full speaker. His father 
spoke Dalabon, his mother Rembarrnga. It is likely that he spoke Rembarrnga as well . 
Jimmy did not always distinguish English from Kriol. His English was hesitant and he 
wasn
1
t literate. 
Nikipini Daluk [ skin name: Belinj] 
?1945 or before? 
Nikipini Daluk, a member of the Marrku Dalabon clan, was born in Maranboy (close to 
Barunga), and lived there for some time with her close family. She reports not using 
English or Kriol in Maranboy. They moved to Barunga when she was still a child, to join 
another part of the family. Other languages were spoken there. Immediately after the 
Northern Territory Land Right Act 1976 was passed, they went back to the Bulman region, 
to Dalabon country .. Weemol had just been opened up, and Nikipini1s family arrived before 
most other families. With her husband and her extended family, she lived between the 
Dalangarr outstation and Weemol for many years, at least until the end of the 1990's, 
before moving back to Beswick. 
,..., 521,..., 
[PDF PAGE 547]
Dalabon is Nikipini Daluk's first native language. She is a full speaker, and is sometimes 
more at-ease in Dalabon than in Kriol. She reports learning Kriol at a later age by listening 
to other people. She never attended school, is not literate, and speaks limited English. She 
understands and speaks Rembarrnga, but identifies strongly with Dalabon and does not 
claim significant knowledge of Rembarrnga. 
Philip Ashley [skin name: Balang] 
c. 1950? 
Philip Ashley, a member of the Balenjkarra (?) clan (a Rembarrnga clan?), was born at 
Joe's Garden, a peanut farm in Katherine, where his parents worked. They moved to 
Barunga, where he went to school. There Philip married June Jolly-Ashley, who has strong 
Dalabon affiliations on her father's side. After the Northern Territory Land Rights Act 1976 
was passed, Philip followed her and her father Jolly Laiwanga to Dalabon country, where 
they were involved in opening up the Dalangarr outstation. They lived between the 
outstation and Weemol with their children for some years, then mostly in Weemol until 
the early 2010, with some extended visits to Beswick and Lake Evella (to the north-east, 
where Philip also has ties). In the early 2010s, they moved to Beswick more permanently. 
Philip Ashley grew up learning Kriol and some English in Katherine, as well as 
Rembarrnga, his father's language, and Dalabon, his mother's language. Philip Ashley 
associates himself with the Rembarrnga group. He seems very fluent in Rembarrnga. 
While not a full speaker of Dalabon, he does enjoy significant mastery. He also speaks 
English well, and he can read and write, albeit with some disfluency. 
June Jolly-Ashley [skin name: Bulanjdjan] 
1963 
June Jolly-Ashley, a member of the Bulaldjdja Dalabon clan, was born in Katherine hospital. 
· She is the daughter of a prominent Dalabon elder, Jolly Laiwanga, deceased in 1998 (and 
since Jimmy Wesan was Jolly's brother, he is also June's classificatory father). June grew up 
in Barunga, learning Kriol. She went to school, probably regularly for a few years, until she 
got married to Philip Ashley. Philip and June had their first children in Barunga. After the 
Northern Territory Land Right Acts 1976, they followed June's father back to Dalabon 
land, where they were involved in opening up the Dalangarr outstation. June and Philip 
lived between the outstation and Weemol with their children for some years, then mostly 
in Weemol until the early 2010s, with some extended visits to Beswick and Lake Evella (to 
the north-east, where Philip also has ties). In the early 2010s, they moved to Beswick more 
permanently. 
June Jolly-Ashley's first and main language is Kriol, a language she is proud of. She is a 
semi-speaker of Dalabon with limited fluency. Her understanding of Dalabon is probably 
much higher than her speaking abilities. June reports starting to learn more Dalabon when 
she got married. She also speaks English, with some disfluency. She can read and write, 
albeit with some effort. She married Philip Ashley when she was fairly young, which, . she 
explains, prevented her from attending high school.
